Mode contract

recorded (outcome.json contract field)

Verbatim, as recorded with the run and sent to the agents.

- primitive to instantiate: `int_sop_4` (precision INT9)
- computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
- input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
- output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
- arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
- registers: on `clk`, the block registers its operands (`ax`, `ay`, `bx`, `by`, `cx`, `cy`, `dx`, `dy`) at one clock edge and `result` at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in `result` after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. `chainin` is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches `result` 2 cycles after it is applied. `chainout` is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value `result` loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before `result` shows it.
- reset: `reset` is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
- power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by `reset`; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
- tie-off: `chainin` = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's `chainout` or a constant may drive it); `mode_sigs` = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
- connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. `chainout` reaches only the next block's `chainin`, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.

The design

Baseline: the unmodified raygentop under this run's VPR settings (channel width 300, median of five seeds, 1 to 5) has a worst register-to-register path of 4.84712 ns on its one clock clk (I/O pads not timed) and uses 6 DSP tiles (as packed at seed 1) of the device's 132. Its used logic-block area is 4.7578e+06 minimum-width transistor areas (one DSP tile 253779, one cluster 27905) and its routed wirelength is 25664, so its area x delay x wirelength product, the objective, is 5.91854e+11. Its slowest stage (read off the seed-1 timing report) is in matmult: one hard multiply on a DSP tile (two_mult_18x19) straight into a flip-flop (a product register), no adder and no LUT; wire 1.42 ns into the multiply, 1.21 out. The next slowest stage (read off the seed-1 timing report), in matmult, is the same shape as path 1, one hard multiply on a DSP tile (two_mult_18x19) straight into another product register; wire 1.31 ns into the multiply, 1.21 out, 4.766 ns, so shortening the slowest stage past that point buys nothing on its own. Any path your rewrite creates is compared against that critical path.

Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.
Cost (guidance: go against it only with a reason in the plan)
  • The clock period is the delay of the slowest stage (the logic between one register and the next). A rewrite that does not touch the slowest stage should not be expected to make the design faster, and should not make another stage slower than it.
  • Blocks in series are separate stages. A path through chainout starts at an input register and continues, in the same stage, into what it drives.
  • Moving or adding registers changes stage lengths and when values arrive.
  • Area falls when soft adders and flip-flops move into blocks.
  • A block of this mode takes a DSP tile alone. Synthesis may already have placed the design's multiplies on tiles, so a block that only replaces one saves little: count tiles against the baseline.
  • The block has chain ports: a block's chainout can drive the next block's chainin directly, so a sum can continue from block to block.
Objective

Minimize area × delay × wirelength against the baseline. If you expect no rewrite to lower it, output TIER: NONE. Among rewrites that lower it, choose the one that lowers it most.

Output
Tiers
  • T1: The block replaces the region's arithmetic as it stands: the same operations on the same operands, now inside the block.
  • T2: The region's arithmetic is regrouped to fit the block (products regrouped into the block's sums, registers moved), computing the same values.
  • NONE: No rewrite: no candidate can be rewritten correctly.
Header

Write exactly this header, each key at the start of its own line, then the plan:

TIER: <exactly one of T1, T2, NONE>
REGIONS: <the converted candidate ids, comma-separated; NONE when TIER is NONE>
SHARED_REDUCTION: <the signal or module the converted products are summed in; NONE for a single region>
BLOCKS: <how many blocks the rewrite instantiates, one integer>
TILES: <how many DSP tiles the whole design then uses, one integer>
STAGE_NS: <the delay of the slowest stage the rewrite leaves, in ns, one number>
MAPPING: <which design signals go to which block ports>
PLAN: <the plan, stating everything listed below>

What the plan must state
  • Every candidate region, converted or left, with the reason each is left; candidates that share a reason may be grouped.
  • How many blocks the rewrite adds, and how many DSP tiles the design then uses.
  • The longest series of blocks in any stage and its delay, against the slowest stage.
  • What soft logic leaves which stage, and whether that stage is the slowest.
  • For each converted region, the register stages from its operands to its result, before and after the rewrite.
Output rules
  • Write nothing before the TIER line; read the source first.
  • A reviewer checks the plan automatically and no person reads it, so do not end with a question or an offer.
  • If a change to the design itself, not to the rewrite, would let more of it use the block, you may say so on a line starting DESIGN_CHANGE:. It is reported to the user and does not change your decision.
Reference simulation

After the edit, the framework simulates the edited design against the original with the reference testbench, comparing every output on every cycle. A candidate that does not match is not measured. The testbench (tb_equiv_bilin.v) and the block's behavioural model (int_sop_4.v) are in sim_reference/.

Why this is the same behavior. Originally ul<=u, vl<=v, wl<=8'hFF-u-v, rul<=ru … are loaded at edge k, and i1r<=ul*rul, i2r<=vl*rvl, i3r<=wl*rwl at edge k+1, with r = (i1r+i2r+i3r) combinational: the operands present before edge k reach r after edge k+1. The block's contract is exactly that — operands registered at one edge, result at the next — so the block's input register replaces ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl and its result register replaces i1r…i3b plus the adder tree, with no change in latency. w is the same 8-bit wrapping 8'hFF-u-v the original computed before the wl register (the testbench's ovf-B/ovf-C vectors exercise that wrap), it just now feeds the block's cx register instead of wl. All operands are unsigned and each product is at most 255*127 = 32385, so the block's zero-extension to 9 bits and its exact 18-bit products reproduce the original 15-bit products. The original sums in 15 bits and the block in 64 bits, but only bits [6:0] are taken in both cases, so the differing wrap width is invisible (ovf-A: 64897 → 15-bit 32129 → [6:0]=1, and 64897 mod 128 = 1).

Reset. The module has no reset port and the testbench adds none, so the reset must be derived inside the module from its inputs; a counter or flag would stay X forever because its next state would depend on its own unknown state. rzerol depends only on inputs, so it is known one edge after power-up, and rrst = rzero & rzerol is then known. rrst high just before edge t means the three r-weights are zero both in cycle t and in cycle t-1, hence u*ru+v*rv+w*rw is zero for both; the clear therefore writes exactly the values the block should hold: result=0 is the correct sum for cycle t-1's operands, and the cleared operand registers make the sum loaded at edge t+1 zero, which is the correct sum for cycle t's operands. When rrst is low the block behaves normally, and the operand registers hold either that cycle's operands or zeros whose sum is the correct zero, so equivalence holds from the first edge at which rrst is high onward — not only at start-up. In the testbench the 8-cycle all-zero lead-in makes rrst high from edge 2, well before comparison begins, and the reference's own registers flush to 0 over the same lead-in. The same argument holds independently for g and b.

ASSUMES: the three weights of a colour (ru,rv,rw = shadedata[41:35], [62:56], [20:14]; gu,gv,gw = [34:28], [55:49], [13:7]; bu,bv,bw = [27:21], [48:42], [6:0], line 2012) are zero on two consecutive cycles at least once after power-up, before that colour's output is used. Support: shadedata is driven straight from the top-level input tm3_sram_data_in (line 676, carried through lines 182 and 188), so the weights are all zero whenever the SRAM data bus is idle/zero, which the design's start-up sequence and the testbench's lead-in both provide. Only the block's power-up X depends on this; equivalence after the first clear does not.

Candidates left, and why.

  • matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … 343$23 (all nine): each is a 16x16 product (Ax,Ay,Az,m11…m33 are 16-bit, lines 300–312), far wider than the block's 9-bit operand ports. Splitting one into 9x9 partial products needs the partials weighted by 2^8 and 2^16, and the block sums its four products with no shift and has no port wide enough to carry a pre-shifted operand, so the arithmetic cannot be expressed on this block. They also feed Cx/Cy/Cz <= am11[30:15]+am12[30:15]+am13[30:15] (lines 348–350), a sum of slices of the products, which the block's single 64-bit sum cannot produce either. Left as they are — which also means the design's slowest stage is untouched.

Blocks and tiles. The rewrite adds 3 int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone. The nine bilinearintrp products occupy 3 DSP tiles in the baseline (mult_9x9_fixed_pt, three products per tile), so those 3 tiles are given back and the design still uses 6 of 132 tiles — no tile change, pure soft-logic and wirelength savings.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. No block drives another: each colour's three products fit the block's four product slots, so chainin is tied to 0 and chainout is unused. The in-stage ends at a block input register (+0.019 setup), the block's own stage is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, and the out-stage starts at result (clock-to-Q 0.060). All three are well under the 4.84712 ns critical stage in matmult, and under the 4.766 ns second path.

Stage-by-stage, and what soft logic leaves.

  • Into the blocks. ay/by/cy come from tm3_sram_data_in through the top-level shadedata wiring, i.e. from an I/O pad (not timed). ax/bx/cx come from the u01*/v10* registers through the unchanged selectuv mux and, for cx, the unchanged 8-bit 8'hFF-u-v: 0.060 clock-to-Q + ~1.31 wire + ~1.03 mux + ~1.03 subtract + 1.17 wire into the block + 0.019 setup ≈ 3.6 ns (≈4.0 ns at the sampled maxima). This is the same soft logic the baseline already had ahead of the ul/vl/wl flip-flops; only its endpoint moves. Not the slowest stage.
  • Inside the blocks. 2.219 ns. Not the slowest stage.
  • Out of the blocks. Leaving this stage: the three 3-input adder trees (two soft adder levels, ~1.03 ns each) that computed r/g/b, now inside the block. The stage is now result clock-to-Q 0.060 + ~0.62 wire + the unchanged temp_shadedata* muxes (lines 2265–2267, 2423–2425, 2482–2484) and linearmapinst (line 2011) into their registers — roughly 2 ns shorter than the baseline's equivalent stage. Not the slowest stage.
  • The slowest stage (matmult: a two_mult_18x19 straight into a product register, 4.84712 ns) is not touched and no new stage approaches it, so STAGE_NS stays 4.84712.

Register stages, before and after (identical for each of the nine converted products): before, 2 stages from the module's operands to the output — the ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl stage, then the i1r…i3b product stage, with the 3-input sum combinational after it. After, 2 stages — the block's operand/chainin input register, then the block's result register, with the slice result[6:0] combinational after it. Latency from u/v/ru…bw to r/g/b is unchanged at 2 cycles.

Why the objective falls. Delay is unchanged (the critical stage is in matmult). Area falls: 12 operand registers (87 flip-flops) and 9 product registers (135 flip-flops, 63 if synthesis already trims them to the 7 used bits) plus three two-level adder trees leave the soft fabric, against 3 added flip-flops and roughly 15–20 LUTs of reset logic, with the DSP tile count flat at 6. Wirelength falls with them: the nine wide product nets and the adder-tree nets between the DSP tiles and the clusters disappear, replaced by three 7-bit nets straight off the blocks.

DESIGN_CHANGE: giving bilinearintrp a globalreset input (it is already in scope at the instantiation, line 2012, and resultwriter already uses it) would let the blocks' reset be driven directly by it, dropping the derived rzero/rzerol logic and the ASSUMES above entirely.

1	// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
4	// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
15	// X until the first clear.
16	module int_sop_4 (
17	    input clk,
18	    input reset,
19	    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
20	    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
21	    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
22	    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
23	    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
24	    input [63:0] chainin,
25	    output reg [63:0] result,
26	    output [63:0] chainout
27	);
28	
29	    // stage 1: the input registers
30	    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
31	    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;
32	
33	    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
34	    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
35	    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
36	    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
37	    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
38	    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64
39	
40	    always @(posedge clk) begin
41	        if (reset) begin
42	            result <= 0;
43	            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
44	            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
45	        end
46	        else begin
47	            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
48	            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
49	            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
50	        end
51	    end
52	
53	    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers
54	
55	endmodule

Task

You are the plan reviewer. You did not write this plan. Check it against the design source, the block's contract and the correctness rules; approve it if it violates none.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design

The design source is raygentop.v. The candidate regions the planner was offered:

An id names a product by its module and its multiply. One that ends in (sum_in=<module>) is a product whose sum sits in that other module: the product leaves its own module through a port and is added there, so the arithmetic to convert spans both. A #1, #2 after an id separates instances of the same product that sit in sums of different shapes.

In every row, operation: sop.
In every row, instances: 1.
In every row, register stages between the products and their sum: products registered 1 stage(s) before the sum.
In every row, products in the whole sum this one belongs to: 3 products in one chain of adders.

Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.
Check
  • Every claim the plan makes about the design (who reads a value, a register's reset or enable, widths, cited lines, ASSUMES lines) against the source.
  • That the mapping as described keeps the same behavior.
  • That the plan states everything the planner's output section requires, listed below.

Do not judge cost or style; measurement decides cost.

What the plan must state
  • Every candidate region, converted or left, with the reason each is left; candidates that share a reason may be grouped.
  • How many blocks the rewrite adds, and how many DSP tiles the design then uses.
  • The longest series of blocks in any stage and its delay, against the slowest stage.
  • What soft logic leaves which stage, and whether that stage is the slowest.
  • For each converted region, the register stages from its operands to its result, before and after the rewrite.
Output
  • First line exactly APPROVE or REVISE.
  • If REVISE, for each problem: the rule it violates or the required item it omits, by name; the design lines; what to change.
  • Write nothing before the verdict line; read the source first. The verdict is applied automatically and no person reads it, so do not end with a question or an offer.
The plan

I'll start by reading the design source.

TIER: T1
REGIONS: bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2875$349, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2876$350, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2877$351, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2878$352, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2879$353, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2880$354, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2881$355, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2882$356
SHARED_REDUCTION: bilinearintrp's three output sums — r = i1r+i2r+i3r (line 2884), g = i1g+i2g+i3g (2885), b = i1b+i2b+i3b (2886); three products per sum, one block per sum
BLOCKS: 3
TILES: 6
STAGE_NS: 4.84712
MAPPING:

  • block rsop: ax={1'b0,u}, ay={2'b0,ru}, bx={1'b0,v}, by={2'b0,rv}, cx={1'b0,w} with w = 8'b11111111-u-v, cy={2'b0,rw}, dx=9'b0, dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0, mode_sigs=12'b0, clk=clk, reset=rrst; result[6:0] drives output r, chainout unconnected
  • block gsop: ax={1'b0,u}, ay={2'b0,gu}, bx={1'b0,v}, by={2'b0,gv}, cx={1'b0,w}, cy={2'b0,gw}, dx=9'b0, dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0, mode_sigs=12'b0, clk=clk, reset=grst; result[6:0] drives output g, chainout unconnected
  • block bsop: ax={1'b0,u}, ay={2'b0,bu}, bx={1'b0,v}, by={2'b0,bv}, cx={1'b0,w}, cy={2'b0,bw}, dx=9'b0, dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0, mode_sigs=12'b0, clk=clk, reset=brst; result[6:0] drives output b, chainout unconnected

PLAN:

What to edit — only module bilinearintrp, lines 2762–2887 of raygentop.v. No other module changes; the instantiation at line 2012 keeps its port list (the equivalence testbench binds that list).

1. Keep the combinational selectuv mux (lines 2818–2858) and its reg[7:0] u; reg[7:0] v; declarations exactly as they are.

2. Delete the register declarations ul, vl, wl (2796–2798), i1b, i2b, i3b, i1g, i2g, i3g, i1r, i2r, i3r (2799–2807), rul, rvl, rwl, gul, gvl, gwl, bul, bvl, bwl (2808–2816), the whole always @(posedge clk) block (2860–2883), and the three assign lines 2884–2886. None of these signals is read anywhere else: ul/vl/wl and rul…bwl are read only by the nine products (2874–2882), the nine i* registers only by the three sums, and the sums only by the module outputs r, g, b (the ul/vl at line 2756 belong to the preceding module, not to this one). The outputs r, g, b are the module's only visible values.

3. Add, in the generated-code style of the module (assign, space before ;, few comments):

verilog

        wire[63:0] rres; 
        wire[63:0] gres; 
        wire[63:0] bres;

        wire[63:0] bchain; 
        wire rzero, gzero, bzero, rrst, grst, brst;

        assign rzero = ~(|{ru, rv, rw}) ;
        assign gzero = ~(|{gu, gv, gw}) ;
        assign bzero = ~(|{bu, bv, bw}) ;

        begin

        assign grst = gzero & gzerol ;

        int_sop_4 rsop (.clk(clk), .reset(rrst), .mode_sigs(12'b0), .ax({1'b0, u}), .ay({2'b0, ru}), .bx({1'b0, v}), .by({2'b0, rv}), .cx({1'b0, w}), .cy({2'b0, rw}), .dx(9'b0), .dy(9'b0), .chainin(64'b0), .result(rres), .chainout(rchain));

        int_sop_4 bsop (.clk(clk), .reset(brst), .mode_sigs(12'b0), .ax({1'b0, u}), .ay({2'b0, bu}), .bx({1'b0, v}), .by({2'b0, bv}), .cx({1'b0, w}), .cy({2'b0, bw}), .dx(9'b0), .dy(9'b0), .chainin(64'b0), .result(bres), .chainout(bchain));

        assign g = gres[6:0] ;
        assign b = bres[6:0] ;

rchain/gchain/bchain are left unread, so no chainout reaches general routing; chainin is the constant 0 the tie-off rule allows.

Why this is the same behavior. Originally ul<=u, vl<=v, wl<=8'hFF-u-v, rul<=ru … are loaded at edge k, and i1r<=ul*rul, i2r<=vl*rvl, i3r<=wl*rwl at edge k+1, with r = (i1r+i2r+i3r) combinational: the operands present before edge k reach r after edge k+1. The block's contract is exactly that — operands registered at one edge, result at the next — so the block's input register replaces ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl and its result register replaces i1r…i3b plus the adder tree, with no change in latency. w is the same 8-bit wrapping 8'hFF-u-v the original computed before the wl register (the testbench's ovf-B/ovf-C vectors exercise that wrap), it just now feeds the block's cx register instead of wl. All operands are unsigned and each product is at most 255*127 = 32385, so the block's zero-extension to 9 bits and its exact 18-bit products reproduce the original 15-bit products. The original sums in 15 bits and the block in 64 bits, but only bits [6:0] are taken in both cases, so the differing wrap width is invisible (ovf-A: 64897 → 15-bit 32129 → [6:0]=1, and 64897 mod 128 = 1).

Reset. The module has no reset port and the testbench adds none, so the reset must be derived inside the module from its inputs; a counter or flag would stay X forever because its next state would depend on its own unknown state. rzerol depends only on inputs, so it is known one edge after power-up, and rrst = rzero & rzerol is then known. rrst high just before edge t means the three r-weights are zero both in cycle t and in cycle t-1, hence u*ru+v*rv+w*rw is zero for both; the clear therefore writes exactly the values the block should hold: result=0 is the correct sum for cycle t-1's operands, and the cleared operand registers make the sum loaded at edge t+1 zero, which is the correct sum for cycle t's operands. When rrst is low the block behaves normally, and the operand registers hold either that cycle's operands or zeros whose sum is the correct zero, so equivalence holds from the first edge at which rrst is high onward — not only at start-up. In the testbench the 8-cycle all-zero lead-in makes rrst high from edge 2, well before comparison begins, and the reference's own registers flush to 0 over the same lead-in. The same argument holds independently for g and b.

ASSUMES: the three weights of a colour (ru,rv,rw = shadedata[41:35], [62:56], [20:14]; gu,gv,gw = [34:28], [55:49], [13:7]; bu,bv,bw = [27:21], [48:42], [6:0], line 2012) are zero on two consecutive cycles at least once after power-up, before that colour's output is used. Support: shadedata is driven straight from the top-level input tm3_sram_data_in (line 676, carried through lines 182 and 188), so the weights are all zero whenever the SRAM data bus is idle/zero, which the design's start-up sequence and the testbench's lead-in both provide. Only the block's power-up X depends on this; equivalence after the first clear does not.

Candidates left, and why.

  • matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … 343$23 (all nine): each is a 16x16 product (Ax,Ay,Az,m11…m33 are 16-bit, lines 300–312), far wider than the block's 9-bit operand ports. Splitting one into 9x9 partial products needs the partials weighted by 2^8 and 2^16, and the block sums its four products with no shift and has no port wide enough to carry a pre-shifted operand, so the arithmetic cannot be expressed on this block. They also feed Cx/Cy/Cz <= am11[30:15]+am12[30:15]+am13[30:15] (lines 348–350), a sum of slices of the products, which the block's single 64-bit sum cannot produce either. Left as they are — which also means the design's slowest stage is untouched.

Blocks and tiles. The rewrite adds 3 int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone. The nine bilinearintrp products occupy 3 DSP tiles in the baseline (mult_9x9_fixed_pt, three products per tile), so those 3 tiles are given back and the design still uses 6 of 132 tiles — no tile change, pure soft-logic and wirelength savings.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. No block drives another: each colour's three products fit the block's four product slots, so chainin is tied to 0 and chainout is unused. The in-stage ends at a block input register (+0.019 setup), the block's own stage is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, and the out-stage starts at result (clock-to-Q 0.060). All three are well under the 4.84712 ns critical stage in matmult, and under the 4.766 ns second path.

Stage-by-stage, and what soft logic leaves.

  • Into the blocks. ay/by/cy come from tm3_sram_data_in through the top-level shadedata wiring, i.e. from an I/O pad (not timed). ax/bx/cx come from the u01*/v10* registers through the unchanged selectuv mux and, for cx, the unchanged 8-bit 8'hFF-u-v: 0.060 clock-to-Q + ~1.31 wire + ~1.03 mux + ~1.03 subtract + 1.17 wire into the block + 0.019 setup ≈ 3.6 ns (≈4.0 ns at the sampled maxima). This is the same soft logic the baseline already had ahead of the ul/vl/wl flip-flops; only its endpoint moves. Not the slowest stage.
  • Inside the blocks. 2.219 ns. Not the slowest stage.
  • Out of the blocks. Leaving this stage: the three 3-input adder trees (two soft adder levels, ~1.03 ns each) that computed r/g/b, now inside the block. The stage is now result clock-to-Q 0.060 + ~0.62 wire + the unchanged temp_shadedata* muxes (lines 2265–2267, 2423–2425, 2482–2484) and linearmapinst (line 2011) into their registers — roughly 2 ns shorter than the baseline's equivalent stage. Not the slowest stage.
  • The slowest stage (matmult: a two_mult_18x19 straight into a product register, 4.84712 ns) is not touched and no new stage approaches it, so STAGE_NS stays 4.84712.

Register stages, before and after (identical for each of the nine converted products): before, 2 stages from the module's operands to the output — the ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl stage, then the i1r…i3b product stage, with the 3-input sum combinational after it. After, 2 stages — the block's operand/chainin input register, then the block's result register, with the slice result[6:0] combinational after it. Latency from u/v/ru…bw to r/g/b is unchanged at 2 cycles.

Why the objective falls. Delay is unchanged (the critical stage is in matmult). Area falls: 12 operand registers (87 flip-flops) and 9 product registers (135 flip-flops, 63 if synthesis already trims them to the 7 used bits) plus three two-level adder trees leave the soft fabric, against 3 added flip-flops and roughly 15–20 LUTs of reset logic, with the DSP tile count flat at 6. Wirelength falls with them: the nine wide product nets and the adder-tree nets between the DSP tiles and the clusters disappear, replaced by three 7-bit nets straight off the blocks.

DESIGN_CHANGE: giving bilinearintrp a globalreset input (it is already in scope at the instantiation, line 2012, and resultwriter already uses it) would let the blocks' reset be driven directly by it, dropping the derived rzero/rzerol logic and the ASSUMES above entirely.

Reference simulation

After the edit, the framework simulates the edited design against the original with the reference testbench, comparing every output on every cycle. A candidate that does not match is not measured. The testbench (tb_equiv_bilin.v) and the block's behavioural model (int_sop_4.v) are in sim_reference/.

Outputs r/g/b (2884–2886) are the only visible values, read at 2011 and 2265–2267/2423–2425/2482–2484 via blr/blg/blb — all left outside and unchanged, as is the port list at 2012.
  • Arithmetic: operands are 8-bit u/v/w and 7-bit weights, so every product ≤ 255·127 = 32385 fits the original reg[14:0]; the 15-bit sum truncated to r[6:0] equals the exact sum mod 128, which is what result[6:0] gives (ovf-A/B/C in directed_raygentop_bilin.vh confirm: 64897 → 1, 57425 → 81). The 8-bit wrap of 8'hFF-u-v is preserved by wire[7:0] w.

The ASSUMES line and its cited lines (2012, 676, 182, 188) are accurate.
  • Tie-offs/chaining: every port connected, dx/dy/chainin/mode_sigs tied 0, chainout wires left unread.
  • Candidates: all nine bilinearintrp products converted; the nine matmult products left, with the stated reason matching 300–312 (16-bit operands) and 348–350 (sum of [30:15] slices).
  • Required items (blocks and tiles, longest block series vs slowest stage, soft logic leaving which stage, register stages before/after) are all stated; their numeric values are cost figures left to measurement.

1	// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
4	// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
15	// X until the first clear.
16	module int_sop_4 (
17	    input clk,
18	    input reset,
19	    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
20	    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
21	    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
22	    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
23	    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
24	    input [63:0] chainin,
25	    output reg [63:0] result,
26	    output [63:0] chainout
27	);
28	
29	    // stage 1: the input registers
30	    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
31	    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;
32	
33	    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
34	    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
35	    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
36	    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
37	    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
38	    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64
39	
40	    always @(posedge clk) begin
41	        if (reset) begin
42	            result <= 0;
43	            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
44	            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
45	        end
46	        else begin
47	            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
48	            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
49	            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
50	        end
51	    end
52	
53	    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers
54	
55	endmodule

1	    // raygentop bilinearintrp: the vector shapes of the hand-written testbench of 2026-08-29, kept so
2	    // that its directed corners are the same vectors. vec derives every input from one byte and three
3	    // weights (the way the first testbench did); raw sets every operand to the value named.
4	    task vec; input [7:0] uv; input [2:0] sel; input [6:0] cr, cg, cb; begin
5	        u01a = uv; v01a = uv ^ 8'h5a; u01b = uv + 1; v01b = uv + 2;
6	        u01c = uv + 3; v01c = uv + 4; u10a = ~uv; v10a = uv >> 1;
7	        u10b = uv | 8'h0f; v10b = uv & 8'hf0; u10c = uv + 7; v10c = uv - 3;
8	        selectuv = sel;
9	        ru = cr; rv = cr ^ 7'h2a; rw = cr + 1;
10	        gu = cg; gv = cg + 2; gw = cg - 1;
11	        bu = cb; bv = cb + 3; bw = cb ^ 7'h15;
12	    end endtask
13	    task raw; input [7:0] u, v; input [2:0] sel; input [6:0] w1, w2, w3; begin
14	        u01a = u; v01a = v; u01b = u; v01b = v; u01c = u; v01c = v;
15	        u10a = u; v10a = v; u10b = u; v10b = v; u10c = u; v10c = v;
16	        selectuv = sel;
17	        ru = w1; rv = w2; rw = w3; gu = w1; gv = w2; gw = w3; bu = w1; bv = w2; bw = w3;
18	    end endtask
19	    // overflow probe: a vector whose three products sum past 2^15 (the original's 15-bit sum wraps),
20	    // then three zero cycles with both sides printed
21	    task overflow; input [8*8-1:0] tag; input [7:0] u, v; input [6:0] w1, w2, w3; integer q; begin
22	        tick; raw(u, v, 3'b000, w1, w2, w3);
23	        for (q = 0; q < 3; q = q + 1) begin
24	            tick; set_zero;
25	            $display("%0s +%0d cycles after apply: r ref=%0d dut=%0d g ref=%0d dut=%0d b ref=%0d dut=%0d", tag, q + 1, r_ref, r_dut, g_ref, g_dut, b_ref, b_dut);
26	        end
27	    end endtask

Task

Edit raygentop.v in this directory to carry out the approved plan below: rewrite the regions it names onto the hard block described next. If a step cannot be done as the plan says, stop and say which step and why; do not improvise a different rewrite.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design
  • Regions in the approved plan: bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2875$349, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2876$350, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2877$351, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2878$352, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2879$353, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2880$354, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2881$355, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2882$356. The plan names their shared sum as 'bilinearintrp's three output sums — r = i1r+i2r+i3r (line 2884), g = i1g+i2g+i3g (2885), b = i1b+i2b+i3b (2886); three products per sum, one block per sum'. In the design their products are registered 1 stage(s) before the sum.
Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.
How to work
  • After each edit, run bash check.sh raygentop.v and read its output. If it fails, fix the RTL and run it again.
  • check.sh reads the architecture's declaration of every hard block. Instantiate the block by its name and do not declare it in the design: a design that defines a module of the block's name fails the check.
  • Do not run place-and-route or any VTR command; that is done after you finish.
  • Stop when check.sh passes and its cell census shows the block instances the plan calls for.
Output

PLAN:

What to edit — only module bilinearintrp, lines 2762–2887 of raygentop.v. No other module changes; the instantiation at line 2012 keeps its port list (the equivalence testbench binds that list).

2. Delete the register declarations ul, vl, wl (2796–2798), i1b, i2b, i3b, i1g, i2g, i3g, i1r, i2r, i3r (2799–2807), rul, rvl, rwl, gul, gvl, gwl, bul, bvl, bwl (2808–2816), the whole always @(posedge clk) block (2860–2883), and the three assign lines 2884–2886. rchain/gchain/bchain are left unread, so no chainout reaches general routing; chainin is the constant 0 the tie-off rule allows.

Why this is the same behavior. Originally ul<=u, vl<=v, wl<=8'hFF-u-v, rul<=ru … are loaded at edge k, and i1r<=ul*rul, i2r<=vl*rvl, i3r<=wl*rwl at edge k+1, with r = (i1r+i2r+i3r) combinational: the operands present before edge k reach r after edge k+1. The block's contract is exactly that — operands registered at one edge, result at the next — so the block's input register replaces ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl and its result register replaces i1r…i3b plus the adder tree, with no change in latency. w is the same 8-bit wrapping 8'hFF-u-v the original computed before the wl register (the testbench's ovf-B/ovf-C vectors exercise that wrap), it just now feeds the block's cx register instead of wl. All operands are unsigned and each product is at most 255*127 = 32385, so the block's zero-extension to 9 bits and its exact 18-bit products reproduce the original 15-bit products. The original sums in 15 bits and the block in 64 bits, but only bits [6:0] are taken in both cases, so the differing wrap width is invisible (ovf-A: 64897 → 15-bit 32129 → [6:0]=1, and 64897 mod 128 = 1).

Reset. The module has no reset port and the testbench adds none, so the reset must be derived inside the module from its inputs; a counter or flag would stay X forever because its next state would depend on its own unknown state. rzerol depends only on inputs, so it is known one edge after power-up, and rrst = rzero & rzerol is then known. rrst high just before edge t means the three r-weights are zero both in cycle t and in cycle t-1, hence u*ru+v*rv+w*rw is zero for both; the clear therefore writes exactly the values the block should hold: result=0 is the correct sum for cycle t-1's operands, and the cleared operand registers make the sum loaded at edge t+1 zero, which is the correct sum for cycle t's operands. When rrst is low the block behaves normally, and the operand registers hold either that cycle's operands or zeros whose sum is the correct zero, so equivalence holds from the first edge at which rrst is high onward — not only at start-up. In the testbench the 8-cycle all-zero lead-in makes rrst high from edge 2, well before comparison begins, and the reference's own registers flush to 0 over the same lead-in. The same argument holds independently for g and b.

ASSUMES: the three weights of a colour (ru,rv,rw = shadedata[41:35], [62:56], [20:14]; gu,gv,gw = [34:28], [55:49], [13:7]; bu,bv,bw = [27:21], [48:42], [6:0], line 2012) are zero on two consecutive cycles at least once after power-up, before that colour's output is used. Support: shadedata is driven straight from the top-level input tm3_sram_data_in (line 676, carried through lines 182 and 188), so the weights are all zero whenever the SRAM data bus is idle/zero, which the design's start-up sequence and the testbench's lead-in both provide. Only the block's power-up X depends on this; equivalence after the first clear does not.

Candidates left, and why.

  • matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … 343$23 (all nine): each is a 16x16 product (Ax,Ay,Az,m11…m33 are 16-bit, lines 300–312), far wider than the block's 9-bit operand ports. Splitting one into 9x9 partial products needs the partials weighted by 2^8 and 2^16, and the block sums its four products with no shift and has no port wide enough to carry a pre-shifted operand, so the arithmetic cannot be expressed on this block. They also feed Cx/Cy/Cz <= am11[30:15]+am12[30:15]+am13[30:15] (lines 348–350), a sum of slices of the products, which the block's single 64-bit sum cannot produce either. Left as they are — which also means the design's slowest stage is untouched.

Blocks and tiles. The rewrite adds 3 int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone. The nine bilinearintrp products occupy 3 DSP tiles in the baseline (mult_9x9_fixed_pt, three products per tile), so those 3 tiles are given back and the design still uses 6 of 132 tiles — no tile change, pure soft-logic and wirelength savings.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. No block drives another: each colour's three products fit the block's four product slots, so chainin is tied to 0 and chainout is unused. The in-stage ends at a block input register (+0.019 setup), the block's own stage is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, and the out-stage starts at result (clock-to-Q 0.060). All three are well under the 4.84712 ns critical stage in matmult, and under the 4.766 ns second path.

Stage-by-stage, and what soft logic leaves.

  • Into the blocks. ay/by/cy come from tm3_sram_data_in through the top-level shadedata wiring, i.e. from an I/O pad (not timed). ax/bx/cx come from the u01*/v10* registers through the unchanged selectuv mux and, for cx, the unchanged 8-bit 8'hFF-u-v: 0.060 clock-to-Q + ~1.31 wire + ~1.03 mux + ~1.03 subtract + 1.17 wire into the block + 0.019 setup ≈ 3.6 ns (≈4.0 ns at the sampled maxima). This is the same soft logic the baseline already had ahead of the ul/vl/wl flip-flops; only its endpoint moves. Not the slowest stage.
  • Inside the blocks. 2.219 ns. Not the slowest stage.
  • Out of the blocks. Leaving this stage: the three 3-input adder trees (two soft adder levels, ~1.03 ns each) that computed r/g/b, now inside the block. The stage is now result clock-to-Q 0.060 + ~0.62 wire + the unchanged temp_shadedata* muxes (lines 2265–2267, 2423–2425, 2482–2484) and linearmapinst (line 2011) into their registers — roughly 2 ns shorter than the baseline's equivalent stage. Not the slowest stage.
  • The slowest stage (matmult: a two_mult_18x19 straight into a product register, 4.84712 ns) is not touched and no new stage approaches it, so STAGE_NS stays 4.84712.

Register stages, before and after (identical for each of the nine converted products): before, 2 stages from the module's operands to the output — the ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl stage, then the i1r…i3b product stage, with the 3-input sum combinational after it. After, 2 stages — the block's operand/chainin input register, then the block's result register, with the slice result[6:0] combinational after it. Latency from u/v/ru…bw to r/g/b is unchanged at 2 cycles.

Why the objective falls. Delay is unchanged (the critical stage is in matmult). Area falls: 12 operand registers (87 flip-flops) and 9 product registers (135 flip-flops, 63 if synthesis already trims them to the 7 used bits) plus three two-level adder trees leave the soft fabric, against 3 added flip-flops and roughly 15–20 LUTs of reset logic, with the DSP tile count flat at 6. Wirelength falls with them: the nine wide product nets and the adder-tree nets between the DSP tiles and the clusters disappear, replaced by three 7-bit nets straight off the blocks.

The testbench (tb_equiv_bilin.v) and the block's behavioural model (int_sop_4.v) are in sim_reference/; you may read them, but editing them has no effect on the result.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Inner-loop check: the front end of the real flow, then a cell census. NOT place-and-route.
# usage: bash check.sh <file.v>
# Reads, in the flow's order: blocks.vlib (every hard block of the architecture, declared from its
# models), primitives.vlib (the flow's library of memories, adders and multipliers), then the design;
# then elaborates with the flow's hierarchy check. A module that is not defined, a port name the
# block does not have, or a misspelled block name fails here as it would in the flow. Do not
# declare the target block in the design: blocks.vlib declares it, and a design that defines a module
# of the target block's name fails this check.
# Prints one pass/fail line, then the cell census of the whole design (the last "Number of cells"
# table yosys prints): soft arithmetic as $mul/$add/$sub, registers as $dff*/$sdff*, memories as
# $mem*, muxes as $mux/$pmux, and every instantiated module by name, which is where a hard-block
# instantiation shows up with its instance count.
set -u
f="${1:?usage: check.sh <file.v>}"
here="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
lib=""
[ -f "$here/blocks.vlib" ] && lib="read_verilog -lib $here/blocks.vlib; "
[ -f "$here/primitives.vlib" ] && lib="${lib}read_verilog -nomem2reg $here/primitives.vlib; "
target="$(sed -n 's|^// target block: *\([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$]*\).*|\1|p' "$here/blocks.vlib" 2>/dev/null | head -1)"
if [ -n "$target" ] && grep -Eq "^[[:space:]]*module[[:space:]]+$target([^A-Za-z0-9_$]|$)" "$f"; then
  echo "FAIL: $f defines module $target; blocks.vlib declares it. Remove the module definition and keep the instances."
  exit 1
fi
out="$(yosys -p "${lib}read_verilog -sv -nolatches $f; hierarchy -check -auto-top -purge_lib; proc; opt; stat" 2>&1)"
rc=$?
if [ $rc -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "FAIL: does not synthesize (yosys exit $rc)"
  echo "$out" | grep -iE 'error|warning' | tail -15
  echo "$out" | tail -10
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: synthesizes cleanly"
echo "Cell census (yosys stat, whole design):"
echo "$out" | awk '/Number of cells:/{buf=$0 "\n"; on=1; next}
                   on && /^[[:space:]]+[$A-Za-z_][^[:space:]]*[[:space:]]+[0-9]+[[:space:]]*$/ {buf=buf $0 "\n"; next}
                   on {on=0}
                   END{printf "%s", buf}' \
  | grep -E 'Number of cells|^[[:space:]]+(\$(mul|add|sub|mem|memrd|memwr|dff|dffe|sdff|sdffe|adff|adffe|mux|pmux)|[A-Za-z_])' || true

1	// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
4	// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
15	// X until the first clear.
16	module int_sop_4 (
17	    input clk,
18	    input reset,
19	    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
20	    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
21	    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
22	    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
23	    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
24	    input [63:0] chainin,
25	    output reg [63:0] result,
26	    output [63:0] chainout
27	);
28	
29	    // stage 1: the input registers
30	    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
31	    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;
32	
33	    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
34	    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
35	    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
36	    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
37	    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
38	    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64
39	
40	    always @(posedge clk) begin
41	        if (reset) begin
42	            result <= 0;
43	            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
44	            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
45	        end
46	        else begin
47	            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
48	            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
49	            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
50	        end
51	    end
52	
53	    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers
54	
55	endmodule

Task

You are the acceptance reviewer. You did not plan or write this edit. Check the edit against the approved plan, the block's contract and the correctness rules.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design

The file raygentop.v is the edited design. The edit is the diff below, taken against the original source.

Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.

2. Delete the register declarations ul, vl, wl (2796–2798), i1b, i2b, i3b, i1g, i2g, i3g, i1r, i2r, i3r (2799–2807), rul, rvl, rwl, gul, gvl, gwl, bul, bvl, bwl (2808–2816), the whole always @(posedge clk) block (2860–2883), and the three assign lines 2884–2886. The outputs r, g, b are the module's only visible values.

rchain/gchain/bchain are left unread, so no chainout reaches general routing; chainin is the constant 0 the tie-off rule allows.

Why this is the same behavior. Originally ul<=u, vl<=v, wl<=8'hFF-u-v, rul<=ru … are loaded at edge k, and i1r<=ul*rul, i2r<=vl*rvl, i3r<=wl*rwl at edge k+1, with r = (i1r+i2r+i3r) combinational: the operands present before edge k reach r after edge k+1. The block's contract is exactly that — operands registered at one edge, result at the next — so the block's input register replaces ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl and its result register replaces i1r…i3b plus the adder tree, with no change in latency. w is the same 8-bit wrapping 8'hFF-u-v the original computed before the wl register (the testbench's ovf-B/ovf-C vectors exercise that wrap), it just now feeds the block's cx register instead of wl. All operands are unsigned and each product is at most 255*127 = 32385, so the block's zero-extension to 9 bits and its exact 18-bit products reproduce the original 15-bit products. The original sums in 15 bits and the block in 64 bits, but only bits [6:0] are taken in both cases, so the differing wrap width is invisible (ovf-A: 64897 → 15-bit 32129 → [6:0]=1, and 64897 mod 128 = 1).

Reset. The module has no reset port and the testbench adds none, so the reset must be derived inside the module from its inputs; a counter or flag would stay X forever because its next state would depend on its own unknown state. rzerol depends only on inputs, so it is known one edge after power-up, and rrst = rzero & rzerol is then known. rrst high just before edge t means the three r-weights are zero both in cycle t and in cycle t-1, hence u*ru+v*rv+w*rw is zero for both; the clear therefore writes exactly the values the block should hold: result=0 is the correct sum for cycle t-1's operands, and the cleared operand registers make the sum loaded at edge t+1 zero, which is the correct sum for cycle t's operands. When rrst is low the block behaves normally, and the operand registers hold either that cycle's operands or zeros whose sum is the correct zero, so equivalence holds from the first edge at which rrst is high onward — not only at start-up. In the testbench the 8-cycle all-zero lead-in makes rrst high from edge 2, well before comparison begins, and the reference's own registers flush to 0 over the same lead-in. The same argument holds independently for g and b.

ASSUMES: the three weights of a colour (ru,rv,rw = shadedata[41:35], [62:56], [20:14]; gu,gv,gw = [34:28], [55:49], [13:7]; bu,bv,bw = [27:21], [48:42], [6:0], line 2012) are zero on two consecutive cycles at least once after power-up, before that colour's output is used. Support: shadedata is driven straight from the top-level input tm3_sram_data_in (line 676, carried through lines 182 and 188), so the weights are all zero whenever the SRAM data bus is idle/zero, which the design's start-up sequence and the testbench's lead-in both provide. Only the block's power-up X depends on this; equivalence after the first clear does not.

Candidates left, and why.

  • matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … 343$23 (all nine): each is a 16x16 product (Ax,Ay,Az,m11…m33 are 16-bit, lines 300–312), far wider than the block's 9-bit operand ports. Splitting one into 9x9 partial products needs the partials weighted by 2^8 and 2^16, and the block sums its four products with no shift and has no port wide enough to carry a pre-shifted operand, so the arithmetic cannot be expressed on this block. They also feed Cx/Cy/Cz <= am11[30:15]+am12[30:15]+am13[30:15] (lines 348–350), a sum of slices of the products, which the block's single 64-bit sum cannot produce either. Left as they are — which also means the design's slowest stage is untouched.

Blocks and tiles. The rewrite adds 3 int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone. The nine bilinearintrp products occupy 3 DSP tiles in the baseline (mult_9x9_fixed_pt, three products per tile), so those 3 tiles are given back and the design still uses 6 of 132 tiles — no tile change, pure soft-logic and wirelength savings.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. No block drives another: each colour's three products fit the block's four product slots, so chainin is tied to 0 and chainout is unused. The in-stage ends at a block input register (+0.019 setup), the block's own stage is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, and the out-stage starts at result (clock-to-Q 0.060). All three are well under the 4.84712 ns critical stage in matmult, and under the 4.766 ns second path.

Stage-by-stage, and what soft logic leaves.

  • Into the blocks. ay/by/cy come from tm3_sram_data_in through the top-level shadedata wiring, i.e. from an I/O pad (not timed). ax/bx/cx come from the u01*/v10* registers through the unchanged selectuv mux and, for cx, the unchanged 8-bit 8'hFF-u-v: 0.060 clock-to-Q + ~1.31 wire + ~1.03 mux + ~1.03 subtract + 1.17 wire into the block + 0.019 setup ≈ 3.6 ns (≈4.0 ns at the sampled maxima). This is the same soft logic the baseline already had ahead of the ul/vl/wl flip-flops; only its endpoint moves. Not the slowest stage.
  • Inside the blocks. 2.219 ns. Not the slowest stage.
  • Out of the blocks. Leaving this stage: the three 3-input adder trees (two soft adder levels, ~1.03 ns each) that computed r/g/b, now inside the block. The stage is now result clock-to-Q 0.060 + ~0.62 wire + the unchanged temp_shadedata* muxes (lines 2265–2267, 2423–2425, 2482–2484) and linearmapinst (line 2011) into their registers — roughly 2 ns shorter than the baseline's equivalent stage. Not the slowest stage.
  • The slowest stage (matmult: a two_mult_18x19 straight into a product register, 4.84712 ns) is not touched and no new stage approaches it, so STAGE_NS stays 4.84712.

Register stages, before and after (identical for each of the nine converted products): before, 2 stages from the module's operands to the output — the ul/vl/wl/rul…bwl stage, then the i1r…i3b product stage, with the 3-input sum combinational after it. After, 2 stages — the block's operand/chainin input register, then the block's result register, with the slice result[6:0] combinational after it. Latency from u/v/ru…bw to r/g/b is unchanged at 2 cycles.

Why the objective falls. Delay is unchanged (the critical stage is in matmult). Area falls: 12 operand registers (87 flip-flops) and 9 product registers (135 flip-flops, 63 if synthesis already trims them to the 7 used bits) plus three two-level adder trees leave the soft fabric, against 3 added flip-flops and roughly 15–20 LUTs of reset logic, with the DSP tile count flat at 6. Wirelength falls with them: the nine wide product nets and the adder-tree nets between the DSP tiles and the clusters disappear, replaced by three 7-bit nets straight off the blocks.

DESIGN_CHANGE: giving bilinearintrp a globalreset input (it is already in scope at the instantiation, line 2012, and resultwriter already uses it) would let the blocks' reset be driven directly by it, dropping the derived rzero/rzerol logic and the ASSUMES above entirely.

  • Scope — only bilinearintrp (raygentop.v:2762–2878) changed; the instantiation at raygentop.v:2012 and its positional port list are untouched, and int_sop_4 appears only at raygentop.v:2871–2873. The edit matches the plan's REGIONS/MAPPING line for line (kept the selectuv mux at 2813–2853 and reg[7:0] u/v, deleted the ul/vl/wl, i*, rul…bwl registers and the three sums, added w, the zero-detect reset logic and the three blocks).
  • Ports — all twelve inputs are connected on each instance (clk, reset, mode_sigs, ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy, chainin); unused product terms dx/dy and chainin are tied to 0 as the tie-off rule allows; mode_sigs = 0; rchain/gchain/bchain are declared and read by nothing, so no chainout reaches general routing. result[6:0] drives r/g/b as planned.
  • Terms and arithmetic — w = 8'hFF - u - v (2855) reproduces the original 8-bit wrapping wl before the register. Operands are zero-extended ({1'b0,u}, {2'b0,ru}); each product ≤ 255·127 = 32385 fits the original 15-bit regs exactly, so the block's 18-bit products match. The original sum wrapped at 15 bits, the block at 64, but both are sliced to [6:0], so the wrap width is invisible.
  • Latency — original: operands loaded at edge k, products at edge k+1, sum combinational; block: operands at edge k, result at edge k+1, slice combinational. 2 cycles either way; the log confirms latency offset 0 and 3039/3156 pairs differing under a 1-cycle delay.
  • Reset — rrst = rzero & rzerol (2856, 2862, 2867) is high only when that colour's three weights were zero in both the current and previous cycle. The clear then writes exactly the values the block would otherwise hold: result=0 is the correct sum for the previous cycle's operands, and the zeroed operand registers give the correct zero sum at the next edge; on the first edge with rrst low the block loads normally. Equivalence therefore holds after every clear, not only at start-up. rzerol is driven only by inputs, so it is known after one edge and the rewrite does not rely on its power-up value (either value leads to a clear by edge 2).
  • Visibility — ul/vl/wl, rul…bwl and i1r…i3b had no reader outside the deleted always block (the ul/vl at 2743–2756 belong to the preceding module, which ends at 2761); r/g/b remain the module's only visible values.
  • ASSUMES — stated in the plan with citations (raygentop.v:2012 weight slices, shadedata from tm3_sram_data_in); it bears only on the power-up X window, which the block contract makes unavoidable, and the 8-cycle zero lead-in satisfies it (x_on_dut_only = 0).

1	// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
4	// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
15	// X until the first clear.
16	module int_sop_4 (
17	    input clk,
18	    input reset,
19	    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
20	    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
21	    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
22	    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
23	    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
24	    input [63:0] chainin,
25	    output reg [63:0] result,
26	    output [63:0] chainout
27	);
28	
29	    // stage 1: the input registers
30	    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
31	    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;
32	
33	    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
34	    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
35	    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
36	    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
37	    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
38	    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64
39	
40	    always @(posedge clk) begin
41	        if (reset) begin
42	            result <= 0;
43	            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
44	            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
45	        end
46	        else begin
47	            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
48	            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
49	            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
50	        end
51	    end
52	
53	    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers
54	
55	endmodule

Task

You are the planner. Read the design source, raygentop.v, and decide which of the candidate arithmetic regions listed below to rewrite onto the hard block described next, or that none should be rewritten. Write a plan for the editor, who carries it out; do not edit any file.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design

Baseline: the unmodified raygentop under this run's VPR settings (channel width 300, median of five seeds, 1 to 5) has a worst register-to-register path of 4.84712 ns on its one clock clk (I/O pads not timed) and uses 6 DSP tiles (as packed at seed 1) of the device's 132. Its used logic-block area is 4.7578e+06 minimum-width transistor areas (one DSP tile 253779, one cluster 27905) and its routed wirelength is 25664, so its area x delay x wirelength product, the objective, is 5.91854e+11. Its slowest stage (read off the seed-1 timing report) is in matmult: one hard multiply on a DSP tile (two_mult_18x19) straight into a flip-flop (a product register), no adder and no LUT; wire 1.42 ns into the multiply, 1.21 out. The next slowest stage (read off the seed-1 timing report), in matmult, is the same shape as path 1, one hard multiply on a DSP tile (two_mult_18x19) straight into another product register; wire 1.31 ns into the multiply, 1.21 out, 4.766 ns, so shortening the slowest stage past that point buys nothing on its own. Any path your rewrite creates is compared against that critical path.
