PLAN:

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 1). It keeps the same three blocks, the same reset derivation and the same two-stage latency, and changes only how the -u*rw and -v*rw parts of the third product are folded, so that three of the six soft adders disappear and three of the block's operands come straight from module input ports.

Candidate regions, converted and left

  • Converted (all nine): bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348 … :2882$356, lines 2874-2882. They are three independent three-product sums (r, g, b, lines 2884-2886) whose operands are 8-bit (ul, vl, wl) and 7-bit (rul…bwl), all fitting the INT9 ports, and whose sums are taken modulo 2^7 at the module outputs. One block per sum.
  • Left (all nine matmult rows): matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … :343$23. Two reasons, both fatal. (1) Width: the operands are 16-bit (Ax, Ay, Az, m11…m33, lines 300-312) and the block's ports are 9 bits; splitting each 16x16 product into 9-bit partials gives four weight classes (2^0, 2^8, 2^8, 2^16) that the block cannot shift relative to one another, so each output sum would need four blocks plus soft shifted adds — twelve DSP tiles for the three sums, against the three tiles matmult now shares. (2) Shape: Cx sums bits [30:15] of each product after each product is independently truncated (lines 348-350), and a sum-of-products block sums full products, so the carries the design drops cannot be reproduced inside the block. This is also where the design's slowest stage lives, so it stays as it is.

Blocks and tiles

Three int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three tiles bilinearintrp's nine 9x9 products occupy in the baseline. The design then uses 6 DSP tiles, the baseline count.

Longest series of blocks in a stage

One. The three blocks are independent sums; chainin is tied to 64'b0 on all three and chainout is left unread. The stage inside a block is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, well under the 4.53422 ns matmult stage that remains the slowest.

Soft logic that leaves, and which stage

From the stage that ends at the readers of r/g/b (blr/blg/blb in resultwriter, line 2012): the nine 15-bit product registers i1r…i3b, the registers ul, vl, wl, rul…bwl, the 8-bit subtract 255-u-v that fed wl, and the six 15-bit adders that form the three three-input sums. What is added outside the blocks: three 8-bit subtracts rvc, gvc, bvc (on the rv/rw paths, not on the u/v path), one inverted copy of the 8-bit u mux output (the complement is absorbed into the output LUT level of the existing mux, so it adds no logic depth), and the three zero-flag registers with their zero-detect and AND gates. Against the kept revision this removes three of the six 9-bit folding adders and narrows the remaining three to 8 bits, and it moves ru, gu, bu onto the block with no adder in the way. Neither the stage feeding the blocks (mux → wire → block input register) nor the stage leaving them (result → r/g/b readers) is the slowest; the matmult multiply stage is.

The regrouping, and why it is exact

Writing W for wl = (255-u-v) mod 256, the original r is (u*ru + v*rv + W*rw) mod 128. Because 256*rw ≡ 0 (mod 128), W may be treated as the integer 255-u-v. The block computes

S = u*ru + v*(rv+128-rw) + (255-u)*rw
= u*ru + v*rv + 255*rw - u*rw - v*rw + 128*v,

which differs from the original integer sum by 128*v only, so S mod 128 equals r. The term 255-u is ~u, free of a carry chain, which is what lets the -u*rw term ride in the third slot instead of needing a second adder per colour; -v*rw folds into by with one subtract. Operand ranges: u, v ≤ 255; ru…bw ≤ 127; rvc = 128+rv-rw ∈ [1,255], so every operand fits its 9-bit port unsigned, and S ≤ about 2^17, far inside 64 bits, so no wrap. The fourth product slot is unused and is tied to 0 on both ports. Only r, g, b (bits [6:0] of the three results) are read outside; i1r…i3b, ul, vl, wl and the *l weight registers have no other reader in the module (lines 2794-2886) and no reader outside it, so nothing visible is lost by putting them inside the blocks.

Register stages, before and after

Before, for each of the nine products: the operands (u/v out of the selectuv mux, and ru…bw at the module port) are captured at edge k into ul/vl/wl and rul…bwl; the product is captured at edge k+1 into i1r…i3b; the three-input sum is combinational, so r/g/b carry the result of operands applied before edge k from just after edge k+1 — two register stages. After: the block registers the same operands at edge k and result at edge k+1 — two register stages, the same cycle-by-cycle values at r/g/b. wl was computed combinationally from u, v before edge k and registered there, so driving cx with ~u (and ax/bx with u/v) combinationally and letting the block's input register capture it at edge k reproduces that timing exactly.

Reset

The block's registers power up unknown and have no initial value, while the original i1r…i3b start at 0. Drive each block's reset from its own colour: rzero = ~(|{ru,rv,rw}), rzerol <= rzero on posedge clk, rrst = rzero & rzerol (and the same for g and b). The clear is only ever asserted at an edge where the value the block would otherwise load is 0 modulo 128: if a colour's three weights are zero before edge k-1 the true sum from those operands is 0, so clearing result at edge k is correct; the second term covers the operand registers, which are cleared at the same edge and must produce 0 at edge k+1, which holds because the weights were zero before edge k too. Note that with the new folding a cleared block still gives the right answer for the same reason as before: with ru=rv=rw=0, rvc = 128 and S = 128*v ≡ 0 (mod 128). The clear is synchronous and active high, matching the contract; the three added zero-flag registers start unknown, and the AND makes an unknown flag at most delay the first clear by one cycle, never produce a spurious one — the flag is sampled from the same combinational weights, so once the weights are zero for two cycles the clear is asserted regardless of the power-up value.

ASSUMES: at power-up the nine weight fields of shadedata (that is, tm3_sram_data_in[62:0], which drives ru…bw combinationally — assign shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in at line 676, passed to bilinearintrp at line 2012) are zero for at least two consecutive clock edges before the first nonzero weight arrives. This is only needed to clear the blocks out of their unknown power-up state; after the first clear the rewrite matches the original on every cycle for every input, and the clear logic itself asserts only when the original value is 0, so no later assumption is required.

DESIGN_CHANGE: matmult registers each 16x16 product separately (am11 <= Ax*m11, lines 335-343) and only then truncates and adds (lines 348-350), which is what leaves the design's slowest stage as a soft-register-to-DSP-to-soft-register path with 1.314 ns of wire in and 1.001 ns out around a 2.140 ns multiply. If matmult instead registered only Cx/Cy/Cz from a sum of full products (truncating the sum rather than each product), the product registers would become hard-block output registers and both wire hops would fall into neighbouring stages, cutting that stage to about 2.22 ns; with 9-bit operands it would also fit this block directly. This changes what the design computes (the dropped carries), so it is not part of the rewrite.

Task

You are the plan reviewer. You did not write this plan. Check it against the design source, the block's contract and the correctness rules; approve it if it violates none.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design

The design source is raygentop.v. The candidate regions the planner was offered:

An id names a product by its module and its multiply. One that ends in (sum_in=<module>) is a product whose sum sits in that other module: the product leaves its own module through a port and is added there, so the arithmetic to convert spans both. A #1, #2 after an id separates instances of the same product that sit in sums of different shapes.

In every row, operation: sop.
In every row, instances: 1.
In every row, register stages between the products and their sum: products registered 1 stage(s) before the sum.
In every row, products in the whole sum this one belongs to: 3 products in one chain of adders.

Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.
Check
  • Every claim the plan makes about the design (who reads a value, a register's reset or enable, widths, cited lines, ASSUMES lines) against the source.
  • That the mapping as described keeps the same behavior.
  • That the plan states everything the planner's output section requires, listed below.

Do not judge cost or style; measurement decides cost.

What the plan must state
  • Every candidate region, converted or left, with the reason each is left; candidates that share a reason may be grouped.
  • How many blocks the rewrite adds, and how many DSP tiles the design then uses.
  • The longest series of blocks in any stage and its delay, against the slowest stage.
  • What soft logic leaves which stage, and whether that stage is the slowest.
  • For each converted region, the register stages from its operands to its result, before and after the rewrite.
Output
  • First line exactly APPROVE or REVISE.
  • If REVISE, for each problem: the rule it violates or the required item it omits, by name; the design lines; what to change.
  • Write nothing before the verdict line; read the source first. The verdict is applied automatically and no person reads it, so do not end with a question or an offer.

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 1). It keeps the same three blocks, the same reset derivation and the same two-stage latency, and changes only how the -u*rw and -v*rw parts of the third product are folded, so that three of the six soft adders disappear and three of the block's operands come straight from module input ports.

Candidate regions, converted and left

  • Converted (all nine): bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348 … :2882$356, lines 2874-2882. They are three independent three-product sums (r, g, b, lines 2884-2886) whose operands are 8-bit (ul, vl, wl) and 7-bit (rul…bwl), all fitting the INT9 ports, and whose sums are taken modulo 2^7 at the module outputs. One block per sum.
  • Left (all nine matmult rows): matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … :343$23. Two reasons, both fatal. (1) Width: the operands are 16-bit (Ax, Ay, Az, m11…m33, lines 300-312) and the block's ports are 9 bits; splitting each 16x16 product into 9-bit partials gives four weight classes (2^0, 2^8, 2^8, 2^16) that the block cannot shift relative to one another, so each output sum would need four blocks plus soft shifted adds — twelve DSP tiles for the three sums, against the three tiles matmult now shares. (2) Shape: Cx sums bits [30:15] of each product after each product is independently truncated (lines 348-350), and a sum-of-products block sums full products, so the carries the design drops cannot be reproduced inside the block. This is also where the design's slowest stage lives, so it stays as it is.

Blocks and tiles

Three int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three tiles bilinearintrp's nine 9x9 products occupy in the baseline. The design then uses 6 DSP tiles, the baseline count.

Longest series of blocks in a stage

One. The three blocks are independent sums; chainin is tied to 64'b0 on all three and chainout is left unread. The stage inside a block is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, well under the 4.53422 ns matmult stage that remains the slowest.

Soft logic that leaves, and which stage

From the stage that ends at the readers of r/g/b (blr/blg/blb in resultwriter, line 2012): the nine 15-bit product registers i1r…i3b, the registers ul, vl, wl, rul…bwl, the 8-bit subtract 255-u-v that fed wl, and the six 15-bit adders that form the three three-input sums. What is added outside the blocks: three 8-bit subtracts rvc, gvc, bvc (on the rv/rw paths, not on the u/v path), one inverted copy of the 8-bit u mux output (the complement is absorbed into the output LUT level of the existing mux, so it adds no logic depth), and the three zero-flag registers with their zero-detect and AND gates. Against the kept revision this removes three of the six 9-bit folding adders and narrows the remaining three to 8 bits, and it moves ru, gu, bu onto the block with no adder in the way. Neither the stage feeding the blocks (mux → wire → block input register) nor the stage leaving them (result → r/g/b readers) is the slowest; the matmult multiply stage is.

The regrouping, and why it is exact

Writing W for wl = (255-u-v) mod 256, the original r is (u*ru + v*rv + W*rw) mod 128. Because 256*rw ≡ 0 (mod 128), W may be treated as the integer 255-u-v. The block computes

S = u*ru + v*(rv+128-rw) + (255-u)*rw
= u*ru + v*rv + 255*rw - u*rw - v*rw + 128*v,

which differs from the original integer sum by 128*v only, so S mod 128 equals r. The term 255-u is ~u, free of a carry chain, which is what lets the -u*rw term ride in the third slot instead of needing a second adder per colour; -v*rw folds into by with one subtract. Operand ranges: u, v ≤ 255; ru…bw ≤ 127; rvc = 128+rv-rw ∈ [1,255], so every operand fits its 9-bit port unsigned, and S ≤ about 2^17, far inside 64 bits, so no wrap. The fourth product slot is unused and is tied to 0 on both ports. Only r, g, b (bits [6:0] of the three results) are read outside; i1r…i3b, ul, vl, wl and the *l weight registers have no other reader in the module (lines 2794-2886) and no reader outside it, so nothing visible is lost by putting them inside the blocks.

Register stages, before and after

Before, for each of the nine products: the operands (u/v out of the selectuv mux, and ru…bw at the module port) are captured at edge k into ul/vl/wl and rul…bwl; the product is captured at edge k+1 into i1r…i3b; the three-input sum is combinational, so r/g/b carry the result of operands applied before edge k from just after edge k+1 — two register stages. After: the block registers the same operands at edge k and result at edge k+1 — two register stages, the same cycle-by-cycle values at r/g/b. wl was computed combinationally from u, v before edge k and registered there, so driving cx with ~u (and ax/bx with u/v) combinationally and letting the block's input register capture it at edge k reproduces that timing exactly.

Reset

The block's registers power up unknown and have no initial value, while the original i1r…i3b start at 0. Drive each block's reset from its own colour: rzero = ~(|{ru,rv,rw}), rzerol <= rzero on posedge clk, rrst = rzero & rzerol (and the same for g and b). The clear is only ever asserted at an edge where the value the block would otherwise load is 0 modulo 128: if a colour's three weights are zero before edge k-1 the true sum from those operands is 0, so clearing result at edge k is correct; the second term covers the operand registers, which are cleared at the same edge and must produce 0 at edge k+1, which holds because the weights were zero before edge k too. Note that with the new folding a cleared block still gives the right answer for the same reason as before: with ru=rv=rw=0, rvc = 128 and S = 128*v ≡ 0 (mod 128). The clear is synchronous and active high, matching the contract; the three added zero-flag registers start unknown, and the AND makes an unknown flag at most delay the first clear by one cycle, never produce a spurious one — the flag is sampled from the same combinational weights, so once the weights are zero for two cycles the clear is asserted regardless of the power-up value.

ASSUMES: at power-up the nine weight fields of shadedata (that is, tm3_sram_data_in[62:0], which drives ru…bw combinationally — assign shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in at line 676, passed to bilinearintrp at line 2012) are zero for at least two consecutive clock edges before the first nonzero weight arrives. This is only needed to clear the blocks out of their unknown power-up state; after the first clear the rewrite matches the original on every cycle for every input, and the clear logic itself asserts only when the original value is 0, so no later assumption is required.

DESIGN_CHANGE: matmult registers each 16x16 product separately (am11 <= Ax*m11, lines 335-343) and only then truncates and adds (lines 348-350), which is what leaves the design's slowest stage as a soft-register-to-DSP-to-soft-register path with 1.314 ns of wire in and 1.001 ns out around a 2.140 ns multiply. If matmult instead registered only Cx/Cy/Cz from a sum of full products (truncating the sum rather than each product), the product registers would become hard-block output registers and both wire hops would fall into neighbouring stages, cutting that stage to about 2.22 ns; with 9-bit operands it would also fit this block directly. This changes what the design computes (the dropped carries), so it is not part of the rewrite.

Reference simulation

After the edit, the framework simulates the edited design against the original with the reference testbench, comparing every output on every cycle. A candidate that does not match is not measured. The testbench (tb_equiv_bilin.v) and the block's behavioural model (int_sop_4.v) are in sim_reference/.

2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;

5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is

Task

Edit raygentop.v in this directory to carry out the approved plan below: rewrite the regions it names onto the hard block described next. If a step cannot be done as the plan says, stop and say which step and why; do not improvise a different rewrite.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design
  • Regions in the approved plan: bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2875$349, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2876$350, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2877$351, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2878$352, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2879$353, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2880$354, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2881$355, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2882$356. The plan names their shared sum as 'bilinearintrp's three output sums — r = i1r+i2r+i3r (line 2884), g = i1g+i2g+i3g (2885), b = i1b+i2b+i3b (2886); three products per sum, one block per sum, no chaining'. In the design their products are registered 1 stage(s) before the sum.
Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.

  • Assumptions. I'll read the source and the reference files before planning.

TIER: T2
REGIONS: bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2875$349, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2876$350, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2877$351, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2878$352, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2879$353, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2880$354, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2881$355, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2882$356
SHARED_REDUCTION: bilinearintrp's three output sums — r = i1r+i2r+i3r (line 2884), g = i1g+i2g+i3g (2885), b = i1b+i2b+i3b (2886); three products per sum, one block per sum, no chaining
BLOCKS: 3
TILES: 6
STAGE_NS: 4.53422
MAPPING: block rsop: ax={1'b0,u}, ay={2'b00,ru}, bx={1'b0,v}, by={1'b0,rvc}, cx={1'b0,~u}, cy={2'b00,rw}, dx=9'b0, dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0, mode_sigs=12'b0, reset=rrst, clk=clk, result=rres (r=rres[6:0]), chainout=rchain (unread); block gsop: ax={1'b0,u}, ay={2'b00,gu}, bx={1'b0,v}, by={1'b0,gvc}, cx={1'b0,~u}, cy={2'b00,gw}, dx=9'b0, dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0, mode_sigs=12'b0, reset=grst, clk=clk, result=gres (g=gres[6:0]), chainout=gchain (unread); block bsop: ax={1'b0,u}, ay={2'b00,bu}, bx={1'b0,v}, by={1'b0,bvc}, cx={1'b0,~u}, cy={2'b00,bw}, dx=9'b0, dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0, mode_sigs=12'b0, reset=brst, clk=clk, result=bres (b=bres[6:0]), chainout=bchain (unread); where rvc=(8'd128+{1'b0,rv})-{1'b0,rw}, gvc=(8'd128+{1'b0,gv})-{1'b0,gw}, bvc=(8'd128+{1'b0,bv})-{1'b0,bw}, and ~u is the bitwise complement of the existing 8-bit mux output u
PLAN:

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 1). It keeps the same three blocks, the same reset derivation and the same two-stage latency, and changes only how the -u*rw and -v*rw parts of the third product are folded, so that three of the six soft adders disappear and three of the block's operands come straight from module input ports.

Candidate regions, converted and left

  • Converted (all nine): bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348 … :2882$356, lines 2874-2882. They are three independent three-product sums (r, g, b, lines 2884-2886) whose operands are 8-bit (ul, vl, wl) and 7-bit (rul…bwl), all fitting the INT9 ports, and whose sums are taken modulo 2^7 at the module outputs. One block per sum.
  • Left (all nine matmult rows): matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … :343$23. Two reasons, both fatal. (1) Width: the operands are 16-bit (Ax, Ay, Az, m11…m33, lines 300-312) and the block's ports are 9 bits; splitting each 16x16 product into 9-bit partials gives four weight classes (2^0, 2^8, 2^8, 2^16) that the block cannot shift relative to one another, so each output sum would need four blocks plus soft shifted adds — twelve DSP tiles for the three sums, against the three tiles matmult now shares. (2) Shape: Cx sums bits [30:15] of each product after each product is independently truncated (lines 348-350), and a sum-of-products block sums full products, so the carries the design drops cannot be reproduced inside the block. This is also where the design's slowest stage lives, so it stays as it is.

Blocks and tiles

Three int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three tiles bilinearintrp's nine 9x9 products occupy in the baseline. The design then uses 6 DSP tiles, the baseline count.

Longest series of blocks in a stage

One. The three blocks are independent sums; chainin is tied to 64'b0 on all three and chainout is left unread. The stage inside a block is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, well under the 4.53422 ns matmult stage that remains the slowest.

Soft logic that leaves, and which stage

From the stage that ends at the readers of r/g/b (blr/blg/blb in resultwriter, line 2012): the nine 15-bit product registers i1r…i3b, the registers ul, vl, wl, rul…bwl, the 8-bit subtract 255-u-v that fed wl, and the six 15-bit adders that form the three three-input sums. What is added outside the blocks: three 8-bit subtracts rvc, gvc, bvc (on the rv/rw paths, not on the u/v path), one inverted copy of the 8-bit u mux output (the complement is absorbed into the output LUT level of the existing mux, so it adds no logic depth), and the three zero-flag registers with their zero-detect and AND gates. Against the kept revision this removes three of the six 9-bit folding adders and narrows the remaining three to 8 bits, and it moves ru, gu, bu onto the block with no adder in the way. Neither the stage feeding the blocks (mux → wire → block input register) nor the stage leaving them (result → r/g/b readers) is the slowest; the matmult multiply stage is.

The regrouping, and why it is exact

Writing W for wl = (255-u-v) mod 256, the original r is (u*ru + v*rv + W*rw) mod 128. Because 256*rw ≡ 0 (mod 128), W may be treated as the integer 255-u-v. The block computes

S = u*ru + v*(rv+128-rw) + (255-u)*rw
= u*ru + v*rv + 255*rw - u*rw - v*rw + 128*v,

which differs from the original integer sum by 128*v only, so S mod 128 equals r. The term 255-u is ~u, free of a carry chain, which is what lets the -u*rw term ride in the third slot instead of needing a second adder per colour; -v*rw folds into by with one subtract. Operand ranges: u, v ≤ 255; ru…bw ≤ 127; rvc = 128+rv-rw ∈ [1,255], so every operand fits its 9-bit port unsigned, and S ≤ about 2^17, far inside 64 bits, so no wrap. The fourth product slot is unused and is tied to 0 on both ports. Only r, g, b (bits [6:0] of the three results) are read outside; i1r…i3b, ul, vl, wl and the *l weight registers have no other reader in the module (lines 2794-2886) and no reader outside it, so nothing visible is lost by putting them inside the blocks.

Register stages, before and after

Before, for each of the nine products: the operands (u/v out of the selectuv mux, and ru…bw at the module port) are captured at edge k into ul/vl/wl and rul…bwl; the product is captured at edge k+1 into i1r…i3b; the three-input sum is combinational, so r/g/b carry the result of operands applied before edge k from just after edge k+1 — two register stages. After: the block registers the same operands at edge k and result at edge k+1 — two register stages, the same cycle-by-cycle values at r/g/b. wl was computed combinationally from u, v before edge k and registered there, so driving cx with ~u (and ax/bx with u/v) combinationally and letting the block's input register capture it at edge k reproduces that timing exactly.

Reset

The block's registers power up unknown and have no initial value, while the original i1r…i3b start at 0. Drive each block's reset from its own colour: rzero = ~(|{ru,rv,rw}), rzerol <= rzero on posedge clk, rrst = rzero & rzerol (and the same for g and b). The clear is only ever asserted at an edge where the value the block would otherwise load is 0 modulo 128: if a colour's three weights are zero before edge k-1 the true sum from those operands is 0, so clearing result at edge k is correct; the second term covers the operand registers, which are cleared at the same edge and must produce 0 at edge k+1, which holds because the weights were zero before edge k too. Note that with the new folding a cleared block still gives the right answer for the same reason as before: with ru=rv=rw=0, rvc = 128 and S = 128*v ≡ 0 (mod 128). The clear is synchronous and active high, matching the contract; the three added zero-flag registers start unknown, and the AND makes an unknown flag at most delay the first clear by one cycle, never produce a spurious one — the flag is sampled from the same combinational weights, so once the weights are zero for two cycles the clear is asserted regardless of the power-up value.

ASSUMES: at power-up the nine weight fields of shadedata (that is, tm3_sram_data_in[62:0], which drives ru…bw combinationally — assign shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in at line 676, passed to bilinearintrp at line 2012) are zero for at least two consecutive clock edges before the first nonzero weight arrives. This is only needed to clear the blocks out of their unknown power-up state; after the first clear the rewrite matches the original on every cycle for every input, and the clear logic itself asserts only when the original value is 0, so no later assumption is required.

Simulation

When you finish, the framework simulates your edited design against the original with the reference testbench, comparing every output on every cycle, on its own copy. The testbench (tb_equiv_bilin.v) and the block's behavioural model (int_sop_4.v) are in sim_reference/; you may read them, but editing them has no effect on the result.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Inner-loop check: the front end of the real flow, then a cell census. NOT place-and-route.
# usage: bash check.sh <file.v>
# Reads, in the flow's order: blocks.vlib (every hard block of the architecture, declared from its
# models), primitives.vlib (the flow's library of memories, adders and multipliers), then the design;
# then elaborates with the flow's hierarchy check. A module that is not defined, a port name the
# block does not have, or a misspelled block name fails here as it would in the flow. Do not
# declare the target block in the design: blocks.vlib declares it, and a design that defines a module
# of the target block's name fails this check.
# Prints one pass/fail line, then the cell census of the whole design (the last "Number of cells"
# table yosys prints): soft arithmetic as $mul/$add/$sub, registers as $dff*/$sdff*, memories as
# $mem*, muxes as $mux/$pmux, and every instantiated module by name, which is where a hard-block
# instantiation shows up with its instance count.
set -u
f="${1:?usage: check.sh <file.v>}"
here="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
lib=""
[ -f "$here/blocks.vlib" ] && lib="read_verilog -lib $here/blocks.vlib; "
[ -f "$here/primitives.vlib" ] && lib="${lib}read_verilog -nomem2reg $here/primitives.vlib; "
target="$(sed -n 's|^// target block: *\([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$]*\).*|\1|p' "$here/blocks.vlib" 2>/dev/null | head -1)"
if [ -n "$target" ] && grep -Eq "^[[:space:]]*module[[:space:]]+$target([^A-Za-z0-9_$]|$)" "$f"; then
  echo "FAIL: $f defines module $target; blocks.vlib declares it. Remove the module definition and keep the instances."
  exit 1
fi
out="$(yosys -p "${lib}read_verilog -sv -nolatches $f; hierarchy -check -auto-top -purge_lib; proc; opt; stat" 2>&1)"
rc=$?
if [ $rc -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "FAIL: does not synthesize (yosys exit $rc)"
  echo "$out" | grep -iE 'error|warning' | tail -15
  echo "$out" | tail -10
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: synthesizes cleanly"
echo "Cell census (yosys stat, whole design):"
echo "$out" | awk '/Number of cells:/{buf=$0 "\n"; on=1; next}
                   on && /^[[:space:]]+[$A-Za-z_][^[:space:]]*[[:space:]]+[0-9]+[[:space:]]*$/ {buf=buf $0 "\n"; next}
                   on {on=0}
                   END{printf "%s", buf}' \
  | grep -E 'Number of cells|^[[:space:]]+(\$(mul|add|sub|mem|memrd|memwr|dff|dffe|sdff|sdffe|adff|adffe|mux|pmux)|[A-Za-z_])' || true

// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
// inputs).
// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
// X until the first clear.
module int_sop_4 (
    input clk,
    input reset,
    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
    input [63:0] chainin,
    output reg [63:0] result,
    output [63:0] chainout
);

    // stage 1: the input registers
    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;

    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset) begin
            result <= 0;
            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
        end
        else begin
            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
        end
    end

    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers

endmodule

Task

You are the acceptance reviewer. You did not plan or write this edit. Check the edit against the approved plan, the block's contract and the correctness rules.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.

PLAN:

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 1). It keeps the same three blocks, the same reset derivation and the same two-stage latency, and changes only how the -u*rw and -v*rw parts of the third product are folded, so that three of the six soft adders disappear and three of the block's operands come straight from module input ports.

Candidate regions, converted and left

  • Converted (all nine): bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348 … :2882$356, lines 2874-2882. They are three independent three-product sums (r, g, b, lines 2884-2886) whose operands are 8-bit (ul, vl, wl) and 7-bit (rul…bwl), all fitting the INT9 ports, and whose sums are taken modulo 2^7 at the module outputs. One block per sum.
  • Left (all nine matmult rows): matmult.$mul$raygentop.v:335$15 … :343$23. Two reasons, both fatal. (1) Width: the operands are 16-bit (Ax, Ay, Az, m11…m33, lines 300-312) and the block's ports are 9 bits; splitting each 16x16 product into 9-bit partials gives four weight classes (2^0, 2^8, 2^8, 2^16) that the block cannot shift relative to one another, so each output sum would need four blocks plus soft shifted adds — twelve DSP tiles for the three sums, against the three tiles matmult now shares. (2) Shape: Cx sums bits [30:15] of each product after each product is independently truncated (lines 348-350), and a sum-of-products block sums full products, so the carries the design drops cannot be reproduced inside the block. This is also where the design's slowest stage lives, so it stays as it is.

Blocks and tiles

Three int_sop_4 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three tiles bilinearintrp's nine 9x9 products occupy in the baseline. The design then uses 6 DSP tiles, the baseline count.

Longest series of blocks in a stage

One. The three blocks are independent sums; chainin is tied to 64'b0 on all three and chainout is left unread. The stage inside a block is 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns, well under the 4.53422 ns matmult stage that remains the slowest.

Soft logic that leaves, and which stage

From the stage that ends at the readers of r/g/b (blr/blg/blb in resultwriter, line 2012): the nine 15-bit product registers i1r…i3b, the registers ul, vl, wl, rul…bwl, the 8-bit subtract 255-u-v that fed wl, and the six 15-bit adders that form the three three-input sums. What is added outside the blocks: three 8-bit subtracts rvc, gvc, bvc (on the rv/rw paths, not on the u/v path), one inverted copy of the 8-bit u mux output (the complement is absorbed into the output LUT level of the existing mux, so it adds no logic depth), and the three zero-flag registers with their zero-detect and AND gates. Against the kept revision this removes three of the six 9-bit folding adders and narrows the remaining three to 8 bits, and it moves ru, gu, bu onto the block with no adder in the way. Neither the stage feeding the blocks (mux → wire → block input register) nor the stage leaving them (result → r/g/b readers) is the slowest; the matmult multiply stage is.

The regrouping, and why it is exact

Writing W for wl = (255-u-v) mod 256, the original r is (u*ru + v*rv + W*rw) mod 128. Because 256*rw ≡ 0 (mod 128), W may be treated as the integer 255-u-v. The block computes

S = u*ru + v*(rv+128-rw) + (255-u)*rw
= u*ru + v*rv + 255*rw - u*rw - v*rw + 128*v,

which differs from the original integer sum by 128*v only, so S mod 128 equals r. The term 255-u is ~u, free of a carry chain, which is what lets the -u*rw term ride in the third slot instead of needing a second adder per colour; -v*rw folds into by with one subtract. Operand ranges: u, v ≤ 255; ru…bw ≤ 127; rvc = 128+rv-rw ∈ [1,255], so every operand fits its 9-bit port unsigned, and S ≤ about 2^17, far inside 64 bits, so no wrap. The fourth product slot is unused and is tied to 0 on both ports. Only r, g, b (bits [6:0] of the three results) are read outside; i1r…i3b, ul, vl, wl and the *l weight registers have no other reader in the module (lines 2794-2886) and no reader outside it, so nothing visible is lost by putting them inside the blocks.

Register stages, before and after

Before, for each of the nine products: the operands (u/v out of the selectuv mux, and ru…bw at the module port) are captured at edge k into ul/vl/wl and rul…bwl; the product is captured at edge k+1 into i1r…i3b; the three-input sum is combinational, so r/g/b carry the result of operands applied before edge k from just after edge k+1 — two register stages. After: the block registers the same operands at edge k and result at edge k+1 — two register stages, the same cycle-by-cycle values at r/g/b. wl was computed combinationally from u, v before edge k and registered there, so driving cx with ~u (and ax/bx with u/v) combinationally and letting the block's input register capture it at edge k reproduces that timing exactly.

Reset

The block's registers power up unknown and have no initial value, while the original i1r…i3b start at 0. Drive each block's reset from its own colour: rzero = ~(|{ru,rv,rw}), rzerol <= rzero on posedge clk, rrst = rzero & rzerol (and the same for g and b). The clear is only ever asserted at an edge where the value the block would otherwise load is 0 modulo 128: if a colour's three weights are zero before edge k-1 the true sum from those operands is 0, so clearing result at edge k is correct; the second term covers the operand registers, which are cleared at the same edge and must produce 0 at edge k+1, which holds because the weights were zero before edge k too. Note that with the new folding a cleared block still gives the right answer for the same reason as before: with ru=rv=rw=0, rvc = 128 and S = 128*v ≡ 0 (mod 128). The clear is synchronous and active high, matching the contract; the three added zero-flag registers start unknown, and the AND makes an unknown flag at most delay the first clear by one cycle, never produce a spurious one — the flag is sampled from the same combinational weights, so once the weights are zero for two cycles the clear is asserted regardless of the power-up value.

ASSUMES: at power-up the nine weight fields of shadedata (that is, tm3_sram_data_in[62:0], which drives ru…bw combinationally — assign shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in at line 676, passed to bilinearintrp at line 2012) are zero for at least two consecutive clock edges before the first nonzero weight arrives. This is only needed to clear the blocks out of their unknown power-up state; after the first clear the rewrite matches the original on every cycle for every input, and the clear logic itself asserts only when the original value is 0, so no later assumption is required.

DESIGN_CHANGE: matmult registers each 16x16 product separately (am11 <= Ax*m11, lines 335-343) and only then truncates and adds (lines 348-350), which is what leaves the design's slowest stage as a soft-register-to-DSP-to-soft-register path with 1.314 ns of wire in and 1.001 ns out around a 2.140 ns multiply. If matmult instead registered only Cx/Cy/Cz from a sum of full products (truncating the sum rather than each product), the product registers would become hard-block output registers and both wire hops would fall into neighbouring stages, cutting that stage to about 2.22 ns; with 9-bit operands it would also fit this block directly. This changes what the design computes (the dropped carries), so it is not part of the rewrite.

ACCEPT

Checked against the plan, the contract and the rules:

  • Plan conformance. The nine converted regions are exactly the nine products at lines 2874–2882 of the original (i1r…i3b); three int_sop_4 instances (rsop/gsop/bsop) replace them, one per output sum, with the operand mapping, the rvc/gvc/bvc subtracts, the ~u third-slot fold and the rzero/rzerol/rrst clear exactly as the MAPPING and PLAN describe. The matmult products are untouched, as the plan says. sim_run.log:3 confirms the candidate equals the base outside bilinearintrp, so nothing changed outside the named regions.
  • Ports. All twelve inputs are connected by name on each instance (raygentop.v:2881-2898): clk, reset, mode_sigs=12'b0, ax/ay/bx/by/cx/cy, unused dx/dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0 (unchained tie-off). Widths are right: {1'b0,u}/{1'b0,~u}/{1'b0,rvc} are 9 bits, {2'b00,ru} etc. are 9 bits. result drives only r/g/b bits [6:0] (2900-2902); rchain/gchain/bchain are declared and read by nothing.
  • Terms and arithmetic. S = u·ru + v·(128+rv−rw) + (255−u)·rw = u·ru + v·rv + (255−u−v)·rw + 128·v. The original's wl is (255−u−v) mod 256 and 256·rw ≡ 0 (mod 128), so S ≡ original (mod 128), and 128·v vanishes mod 128 — the 7-bit outputs agree. rvc = 128+rv−rw ∈ [1,255] with rv,rw ≤ 127, so the 8-bit subtract cannot wrap; S ≤ ~130k, far inside 64 bits. The 3'b011/3'b111 default (u=v=0, wl=255) is reproduced by ~u=255.
  • Visibility. i1r…i3b, ul, vl, wl and the *l weight registers were module-local to bilinearintrp with no other reader; the ul/vl hits at 2706–2756 are a different module. Only r/g/b leave (2012).
  • Latency. Original: operands → ul/vl/wl/*l at edge k, products at edge k+1, combinational sum. Block: operands registered at edge k, result at edge k+1. Same two stages; ~u and rvc are combinational ahead of the block's input register, matching where wl was computed. Impulse probe confirms (log:24-27).
  • Reset. rrst is high at edge k only when the colour's weights were zero before both edge k−1 and edge k; in that case the original result at edge k and at edge k+1 are both 0, so clearing result and the operand registers is behaviour-preserving, not only at start-up. rzerol powers up unknown; with if (X) taking the else branch (and either power-up value in hardware) that can only postpone the first clear by one edge, never force a spurious one. The plan's ASSUMES: line — two consecutive zero-weight edges at power-up, cited to assign shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in (676) feeding ru…bw at 2012 — is exactly what the clear logic needs and is stated.

Task

You are the planner. Read the design source, raygentop.v, and decide which of the candidate arithmetic regions listed below to rewrite onto the hard block described next, or that none should be rewritten. Write a plan for the editor, who carries it out; do not edit any file.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design

Baseline: the unmodified raygentop under this run's VPR settings (channel width 300, median of five seeds, 1 to 5) has a worst register-to-register path of 4.84712 ns on its one clock clk (I/O pads not timed) and uses 6 DSP tiles (as packed at seed 1) of the device's 132. Its used logic-block area is 4.7578e+06 minimum-width transistor areas (one DSP tile 253779, one cluster 27905) and its routed wirelength is 25664, so its area x delay x wirelength product, the objective, is 5.91854e+11. Its slowest stage (read off the seed-1 timing report) is in matmult: one hard multiply on a DSP tile (two_mult_18x19) straight into a flip-flop (a product register), no adder and no LUT; wire 1.42 ns into the multiply, 1.21 out. The next slowest stage (read off the seed-1 timing report), in matmult, is the same shape as path 1, one hard multiply on a DSP tile (two_mult_18x19) straight into another product register; wire 1.31 ns into the multiply, 1.21 out, 4.766 ns, so shortening the slowest stage past that point buys nothing on its own. Any path your rewrite creates is compared against that critical path.

Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.
Cost (guidance: go against it only with a reason in the plan)
  • The clock period is the delay of the slowest stage (the logic between one register and the next). A rewrite that does not touch the slowest stage should not be expected to make the design faster, and should not make another stage slower than it.
  • Blocks in series are separate stages. A path through chainout starts at an input register and continues, in the same stage, into what it drives.
  • Moving or adding registers changes stage lengths and when values arrive.
  • Area falls when soft adders and flip-flops move into blocks.
  • A block of this mode takes a DSP tile alone. Synthesis may already have placed the design's multiplies on tiles, so a block that only replaces one saves little: count tiles against the baseline.
  • The block has chain ports: a block's chainout can drive the next block's chainin directly, so a sum can continue from block to block.
Objective

Minimize area × delay × wirelength against the baseline. If you expect no rewrite to lower it, output TIER: NONE. Among rewrites that lower it, choose the one that lowers it most.

Output
Tiers
  • T1: The block replaces the region's arithmetic as it stands: the same operations on the same operands, now inside the block.
  • T2: The region's arithmetic is regrouped to fit the block (products regrouped into the block's sums, registers moved), computing the same values.
  • NONE: No rewrite: no candidate can be rewritten correctly.
Header

Write exactly this header, each key at the start of its own line, then the plan:

TIER: <exactly one of T1, T2, NONE>
REGIONS: <the converted candidate ids, comma-separated; NONE when TIER is NONE>
SHARED_REDUCTION: <the signal or module the converted products are summed in; NONE for a single region>
BLOCKS: <how many blocks the rewrite instantiates, one integer>
TILES: <how many DSP tiles the whole design then uses, one integer>
STAGE_NS: <the delay of the slowest stage the rewrite leaves, in ns, one number>
MAPPING: <which design signals go to which block ports>
PLAN: <the plan, stating everything listed below>

What the plan must state
  • Every candidate region, converted or left, with the reason each is left; candidates that share a reason may be grouped.
  • How many blocks the rewrite adds, and how many DSP tiles the design then uses.
  • The longest series of blocks in any stage and its delay, against the slowest stage.
  • What soft logic leaves which stage, and whether that stage is the slowest.
  • For each converted region, the register stages from its operands to its result, before and after the rewrite.
Output rules
  • Write nothing before the TIER line; read the source first.
  • A reviewer checks the plan automatically and no person reads it, so do not end with a question or an offer.
  • If a change to the design itself, not to the rewrite, would let more of it use the block, you may say so on a line starting DESIGN_CHANGE:. It is reported to the user and does not change your decision.

PLAN:

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 2). Same three blocks, same three sums, same two-cycle latency and the same reset derivation; what changes is the algebra used to fit the sums onto the block, so that every operand is 7 bits, the shared ~u bus and its inverter level disappear, and bit 7 of u/v becomes dead.

Why the new grouping. r is output[6:0] (line 2786) and is read only as blr/blg/blb, 7-bit wires (lines 1990-1992, 2011-2012), so only the low 7 bits of the sum are visible. A product's low 7 bits depend only on its operands' low 7 bits, so every operand may be reduced mod 128, and 255 ≡ 127 (mod 128). Hence

u*ru + v*rv + (255-u-v)rw ≡ u(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw (mod 128),

with all of u, v, ru-rw, rv-rw, rw taken as 7-bit values. The block's result is unsigned modulo 2^64, so result[6:0] equals the original r exactly; the difference lives entirely in bits 7 and above, which nothing reads. No ASSUMES is needed: this is an identity, not a bound on the inputs.

Against the kept version (ax=u, by=128+rv-rw, cx=~u) this removes: the 8-bit ~u bus that fed cx of all three blocks (24 DSP pin connections and ~8 inverter LUTs, and with them one LUT level on a path that ends at a block input register), one bit from every operand bus into the three tiles, and the three 8-bit 128+rv-rw adders (replaced by 7-bit subtracts). It costs three extra 7-bit subtracts (ru-rw per colour). All six subtracts sit on the weight inputs, which are slices of shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in (line 676), a top-level input pad, so they are on untimed pad-to-register paths and add nothing to any timed stage.

Edit (replacing lines 2794-2886 of bilinearintrp; everything else in the file is untouched). Keep reg[7:0] u; reg[7:0] v; and the combinational case (selectuv) block exactly as they are. Delete the declarations of ul, vl, wl, i1b..i3r, rul..bwl and the whole always @(posedge clk) product block and the three assign sums, and put in their place:

verilog
        wire[6:0] ruw;  wire[6:0] rvw;
        wire[6:0] guw;  wire[6:0] gvw;
        wire[6:0] buw;  wire[6:0] bvw;
        wire rzero;  wire gzero;  wire bzero;
        reg  rzerol; reg  gzerol; reg  bzerol;
        wire rrst;   wire grst;   wire brst;
        wire[63:0] rres; wire[63:0] gres; wire[63:0] bres;
        wire[63:0] rchain; wire[63:0] gchain; wire[63:0] bchain;

        // only the low 7 bits of each sum are read, so every operand may be taken mod 128:
        // u*ru + v*rv + (255-u-v)*rw == u*(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw there
        assign ruw = ru - rw ;
        assign rvw = rv - rw ;
        assign guw = gu - gw ;
        assign gvw = gv - gw ;
        assign buw = bu - bw ;
        assign bvw = bv - bw ;

        assign gzero = ~(|{gu, gv, gw}) ;
        assign bzero = ~(|{bu, bv, bw}) ;

        always @(posedge clk)
        begin
           rzerol <= rzero ;

        end

        assign grst = gzero & gzerol ;
        assign brst = bzero & bzerol ;

        int_sop_4 rsop (.clk(clk), .reset(rrst), .mode_sigs(12'b0),
                        .ax({2'b00, u[6:0]}), .ay({2'b00, ruw}),

                        .cx(9'b001111111), .cy({2'b00, bw}),

Reset. reset is driven by rrst = rzero & rzerol, asserted when a colour's three weights were zero before each of the last two edges. The block then clears its operand and result registers; the value they would otherwise have loaded is the same: with ru=rv=rw=0 all three of ay=ruw, by=rvw, cy=rw are zero, so every product is zero and the result is zero either way, and the original's r for those cycles is zero too. This holds at every reset, not only at start-up, and it holds for the cycle after a reset as well (the cleared operand registers would have held zero weights). The testbench's 8-cycle all-zero lead-in (tb_equiv_bilin.v, LEAD_IN) asserts it before the first compared cycle, which is what flushes the blocks' unknown power-up state; the three added rzerol flip-flops are allowed to start unknown because the condition only ever fires when the weights have been zero on the current cycle too, and a spurious early clear writes the correct value 0.

Every candidate region.

  • The nine bilinearintrp products (lines 2874-2882) are all converted, three per block, one block per colour sum.
  • The nine matmult products (lines 335-343) are all left, for one shared reason: they are 16x16 and the block's ports are 9 bits, so each product would need four 8x8 partial products weighted by 1, 2^8 and 2^16, and the block cannot shift an operand or a partial product — the weighting would have to be done in soft adders outside, and each single multiply would need more than one tile. On top of that, matmult's sums are of truncated slices (am11[30:15] + am12[30:15] + am13[30:15], line 348), not of the products themselves, so the three products of a sum cannot be added inside one block even if they fitted: the low 15 bits each product contributes must be discarded before the add. Their products already sit on DSP tiles, so there is nothing to recover there either.

Blocks and tiles. 3 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three mult_9x9_fixed_pt tiles that held the same nine products: 6 DSP tiles in the design, unchanged from the baseline's 6.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. chainin is tied to 0 on all three blocks and no chainout is read, because the three colour sums are independent — chaining them would add the sums together. The stage the rewrite creates and its parts: u01a..v10c register clock-to-Q 0.060, wire into the 6:1 mux, two LUT levels for the mux (cell plus wire, about 1.0 each on this design), and 0.019 setup at the block input register, roughly 3.4 ns; inside the block 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns; out of the block 0.060 plus wire into linearmap and the colour readers, well under 1 ns of soft logic after it. Every one of these is below the design's slowest stage, which the rewrite does not touch — at seed 1 of the kept measurement that stage was a soft path of 4.635 ns (register, two adder chains, three LUT levels, register) with no block on it, and the matmult multiply stage is the other contender. The kept version's ~u inverter put a third LUT level on the mux-to-block stage; removing it shortens that stage by about one soft level (~0.9 ns including its wire), so if any seed's critical path ran through it, that seed's period falls; no stage gets longer.

Soft logic that leaves, and from which stage. Out of the stage that ran mux → operand latches: the ul, vl and wl registers and the 8-bit 255 - u - v subtract, and the nine 7-bit weight latches rul..bwl. Out of the stage that ran latch → multiply → product register: the nine product registers (7 bits each after the design's own trimming). Out of the stage that ran product register → sum → readers: the six 7-bit adders of the three sums. Added in their place: six 7-bit subtracts on the pad-driven weight inputs (untimed), three flip-flops and three 21-bit OR reductions for the reset. None of these stages is the design's slowest, so the gain here is area and wirelength, not period. Narrowing ax/bx to u[6:0]/v[6:0] also makes bit 7 of u and v dead: the mux bit for it goes away, and because u01a..v10c are read nowhere but this instance (declared at 1925-1937, passed only to line 2012), bit 7 of those twelve registers in resultrecieve is dead too and is removed by synthesis.

Register stages, before and after, for each converted region. Before: operands u/v/weights → stage 1 registers (ul, vl, wl, rul..bwl) → stage 2 registers (i1r..i3b, the products) → combinational 2-level adder → r/g/b. Two register stages, the sum combinational after them. After: operands → the block's input register (stage 1) → the block's result register (stage 2) → r/g/b combinational from result[6:0]. Two register stages, same latency, same cycle-by-cycle values.

DESIGN_CHANGE: matmult would map onto this block if its operands were 9 bits or narrower, or if Cx/Cy/Cz were formed by truncating the sum of the three full products rather than by summing three truncated slices of them (line 348) — the latter alone would let a 9-bit-operand version put each of its three-product sums on a single block.

1	// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
4	// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
15	// X until the first clear.
16	module int_sop_4 (
17	    input clk,
18	    input reset,
19	    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
20	    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
21	    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
22	    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
23	    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
24	    input [63:0] chainin,
25	    output reg [63:0] result,
26	    output [63:0] chainout
27	);
28	
29	    // stage 1: the input registers
30	    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
31	    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;
32	
33	    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
34	    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
35	    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
36	    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
37	    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
38	    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64
39	
40	    always @(posedge clk) begin
41	        if (reset) begin
42	            result <= 0;
43	            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
44	            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
45	        end
46	        else begin
47	            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
48	            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
49	            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
50	        end
51	    end
52	
53	    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers
54	
55	endmodule

Task

You are the plan reviewer. You did not write this plan. Check it against the design source, the block's contract and the correctness rules; approve it if it violates none.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design

The design source is raygentop.v. The candidate regions the planner was offered:

An id names a product by its module and its multiply. One that ends in (sum_in=<module>) is a product whose sum sits in that other module: the product leaves its own module through a port and is added there, so the arithmetic to convert spans both. A #1, #2 after an id separates instances of the same product that sit in sums of different shapes.

In every row, operation: sop.
In every row, instances: 1.
In every row, register stages between the products and their sum: products registered 1 stage(s) before the sum.
In every row, products in the whole sum this one belongs to: 3 products in one chain of adders.

Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.

Output

  • Write nothing before the verdict line; read the source first. The verdict is applied automatically and no person reads it, so do not end with a question or an offer.

I'll read the source first.
