PLAN:

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 2). Same three blocks, same three sums, same two-cycle latency and the same reset derivation; what changes is the algebra used to fit the sums onto the block, so that every operand is 7 bits, the shared ~u bus and its inverter level disappear, and bit 7 of u/v becomes dead.

Why the new grouping. r is output[6:0] (line 2786) and is read only as blr/blg/blb, 7-bit wires (lines 1990-1992, 2011-2012), so only the low 7 bits of the sum are visible. A product's low 7 bits depend only on its operands' low 7 bits, so every operand may be reduced mod 128, and 255 ≡ 127 (mod 128). Hence

u*ru + v*rv + (255-u-v)rw ≡ u(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw (mod 128),

with all of u, v, ru-rw, rv-rw, rw taken as 7-bit values. The block's result is unsigned modulo 2^64, so result[6:0] equals the original r exactly; the difference lives entirely in bits 7 and above, which nothing reads. No ASSUMES is needed: this is an identity, not a bound on the inputs.

Against the kept version (ax=u, by=128+rv-rw, cx=~u) this removes: the 8-bit ~u bus that fed cx of all three blocks (24 DSP pin connections and ~8 inverter LUTs, and with them one LUT level on a path that ends at a block input register), one bit from every operand bus into the three tiles, and the three 8-bit 128+rv-rw adders (replaced by 7-bit subtracts). It costs three extra 7-bit subtracts (ru-rw per colour). All six subtracts sit on the weight inputs, which are slices of shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in (line 676), a top-level input pad, so they are on untimed pad-to-register paths and add nothing to any timed stage.

Edit (replacing lines 2794-2886 of bilinearintrp; everything else in the file is untouched). Keep reg[7:0] u; reg[7:0] v; and the combinational case (selectuv) block exactly as they are. Delete the declarations of ul, vl, wl, i1b..i3r, rul..bwl and the whole always @(posedge clk) product block and the three assign sums, and put in their place:

verilog
        wire[6:0] ruw;  wire[6:0] rvw;
        wire[6:0] guw;  wire[6:0] gvw;
        wire[6:0] buw;  wire[6:0] bvw;
        wire rzero;  wire gzero;  wire bzero;
        reg  rzerol; reg  gzerol; reg  bzerol;
        wire rrst;   wire grst;   wire brst;
        wire[63:0] rres; wire[63:0] gres; wire[63:0] bres;
        wire[63:0] rchain; wire[63:0] gchain; wire[63:0] bchain;

        // only the low 7 bits of each sum are read, so every operand may be taken mod 128:
        // u*ru + v*rv + (255-u-v)*rw == u*(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw there
        assign ruw = ru - rw ;
        assign rvw = rv - rw ;
        assign guw = gu - gw ;
        assign gvw = gv - gw ;
        assign buw = bu - bw ;
        assign bvw = bv - bw ;

        // the blocks power up unknown, so clear them whenever a colour's weights have been
        // zero for two cycles: every operand of that colour is then zero anyway
        assign rzero = ~(|{ru, rv, rw}) ;
        assign gzero = ~(|{gu, gv, gw}) ;
        assign bzero = ~(|{bu, bv, bw}) ;

        always @(posedge clk)
        begin
           rzerol <= rzero ;
           gzerol <= gzero ;
           bzerol <= bzero ;
        end

        assign rrst = rzero & rzerol ;
        assign grst = gzero & gzerol ;
        assign brst = bzero & bzerol ;

        int_sop_4 rsop (.clk(clk), .reset(rrst), .mode_sigs(12'b0),
                        .ax({2'b00, u[6:0]}), .ay({2'b00, ruw}),
                        .bx({2'b00, v[6:0]}), .by({2'b00, rvw}),
                        .cx(9'b001111111), .cy({2'b00, rw}),
                        .dx(9'b0), .dy(9'b0), .chainin(64'b0),
                        .result(rres), .chainout(rchain)) ;
        int_sop_4 gsop (.clk(clk), .reset(grst), .mode_sigs(12'b0),
                        .ax({2'b00, u[6:0]}), .ay({2'b00, guw}),
                        .bx({2'b00, v[6:0]}), .by({2'b00, gvw}),
                        .cx(9'b001111111), .cy({2'b00, gw}),
                        .dx(9'b0), .dy(9'b0), .chainin(64'b0),
                        .result(gres), .chainout(gchain)) ;
        int_sop_4 bsop (.clk(clk), .reset(brst), .mode_sigs(12'b0),
                        .ax({2'b00, u[6:0]}), .ay({2'b00, buw}),
                        .bx({2'b00, v[6:0]}), .by({2'b00, bvw}),
                        .cx(9'b001111111), .cy({2'b00, bw}),
                        .dx(9'b0), .dy(9'b0), .chainin(64'b0),
                        .result(bres), .chainout(bchain)) ;

        assign r = rres[6:0] ;
        assign g = gres[6:0] ;
        assign b = bres[6:0] ;

Reset. reset is driven by rrst = rzero & rzerol, asserted when a colour's three weights were zero before each of the last two edges. The block then clears its operand and result registers; the value they would otherwise have loaded is the same: with ru=rv=rw=0 all three of ay=ruw, by=rvw, cy=rw are zero, so every product is zero and the result is zero either way, and the original's r for those cycles is zero too. This holds at every reset, not only at start-up, and it holds for the cycle after a reset as well (the cleared operand registers would have held zero weights). The testbench's 8-cycle all-zero lead-in (tb_equiv_bilin.v, LEAD_IN) asserts it before the first compared cycle, which is what flushes the blocks' unknown power-up state; the three added rzerol flip-flops are allowed to start unknown because the condition only ever fires when the weights have been zero on the current cycle too, and a spurious early clear writes the correct value 0.

Every candidate region.

  • The nine bilinearintrp products (lines 2874-2882) are all converted, three per block, one block per colour sum.
  • The nine matmult products (lines 335-343) are all left, for one shared reason: they are 16x16 and the block's ports are 9 bits, so each product would need four 8x8 partial products weighted by 1, 2^8 and 2^16, and the block cannot shift an operand or a partial product — the weighting would have to be done in soft adders outside, and each single multiply would need more than one tile. On top of that, matmult's sums are of truncated slices (am11[30:15] + am12[30:15] + am13[30:15], line 348), not of the products themselves, so the three products of a sum cannot be added inside one block even if they fitted: the low 15 bits each product contributes must be discarded before the add. Their products already sit on DSP tiles, so there is nothing to recover there either.

Blocks and tiles. 3 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three mult_9x9_fixed_pt tiles that held the same nine products: 6 DSP tiles in the design, unchanged from the baseline's 6.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. chainin is tied to 0 on all three blocks and no chainout is read, because the three colour sums are independent — chaining them would add the sums together. The stage the rewrite creates and its parts: u01a..v10c register clock-to-Q 0.060, wire into the 6:1 mux, two LUT levels for the mux (cell plus wire, about 1.0 each on this design), and 0.019 setup at the block input register, roughly 3.4 ns; inside the block 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns; out of the block 0.060 plus wire into linearmap and the colour readers, well under 1 ns of soft logic after it. Every one of these is below the design's slowest stage, which the rewrite does not touch — at seed 1 of the kept measurement that stage was a soft path of 4.635 ns (register, two adder chains, three LUT levels, register) with no block on it, and the matmult multiply stage is the other contender. The kept version's ~u inverter put a third LUT level on the mux-to-block stage; removing it shortens that stage by about one soft level (~0.9 ns including its wire), so if any seed's critical path ran through it, that seed's period falls; no stage gets longer.

Soft logic that leaves, and from which stage. Out of the stage that ran mux → operand latches: the ul, vl and wl registers and the 8-bit 255 - u - v subtract, and the nine 7-bit weight latches rul..bwl. Out of the stage that ran latch → multiply → product register: the nine product registers (7 bits each after the design's own trimming). Out of the stage that ran product register → sum → readers: the six 7-bit adders of the three sums. Added in their place: six 7-bit subtracts on the pad-driven weight inputs (untimed), three flip-flops and three 21-bit OR reductions for the reset. None of these stages is the design's slowest, so the gain here is area and wirelength, not period. Narrowing ax/bx to u[6:0]/v[6:0] also makes bit 7 of u and v dead: the mux bit for it goes away, and because u01a..v10c are read nowhere but this instance (declared at 1925-1937, passed only to line 2012), bit 7 of those twelve registers in resultrecieve is dead too and is removed by synthesis.

Register stages, before and after, for each converted region. Before: operands u/v/weights → stage 1 registers (ul, vl, wl, rul..bwl) → stage 2 registers (i1r..i3b, the products) → combinational 2-level adder → r/g/b. Two register stages, the sum combinational after them. After: operands → the block's input register (stage 1) → the block's result register (stage 2) → r/g/b combinational from result[6:0]. Two register stages, same latency, same cycle-by-cycle values.

DESIGN_CHANGE: matmult would map onto this block if its operands were 9 bits or narrower, or if Cx/Cy/Cz were formed by truncating the sum of the three full products rather than by summing three truncated slices of them (line 348) — the latter alone would let a 9-bit-operand version put each of its three-product sums on a single block.

Reference simulation

After the edit, the framework simulates the edited design against the original with the reference testbench, comparing every output on every cycle. A candidate that does not match is not measured. The testbench (tb_equiv_bilin.v) and the block's behavioural model (int_sop_4.v) are in sim_reference/.

response

I'll read the source and the reference files before judging.

APPROVE

The algebra, the register alignment, the reset derivation and every design claim check out against raygentop.v:

  • Identity. r/g/b are output[6:0] (lines 2786-2791) and the sums at 2884-2886 are truncated to 7 bits on assignment, so only mod 128 matters. wl = 8'b11111111 - u - v (2862) wraps mod 256, so wl ≡ 127-u-v (mod 128), and u*ru + v*rv + wl*rw ≡ u*(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw (mod 128) with all factors reduced to 7 bits. The 9×9 products are exact (≤127·127) and the block's 64-bit sum wraps only above bit 63, so result[6:0] equals the original r exactly. No ASSUMES is needed; no bound on inputs is used.
  • Visibility. The only readers of the module's outputs are blr/blg/blb, 7-bit wires (1990-1992), consumed by linearmap (2011) and by the 7-bit fields of temp_shadedataa/b/c (2265-2267, 2423-2425, 2482-2484). The 15-bit i1r..i3b and the latches ul,vl,wl,rul..bwl are local to bilinearintrp (2796-2816) and read nowhere else, so dropping their upper bits is invisible. u01a..v10c are produced by resultrecieve (line 186) and consumed only by this instance (188 → 2012), so the dead bit-7 claim is accurate.
  • Registers. Original: operands → ul/vl/wl/weight latches (edge k) → product regs (edge k+1) → combinational 3-input add; block: operands → input regs (edge k) → result reg (edge k+1) → result[6:0]. Both operands of every product (including wl's dependence on u,v) are sampled at the same edge in both versions, so the cycle-by-cycle values match.
  • Reset. rrst = rzero & rzerol is high at edge k only if all three weights were zero before edge k and before edge k−1. Then ay=ruw, by=rvw, cy=rw loaded at k−1 are all 0, so the result the clear discards is 0; the operand clear at k is harmless because the y-operands it replaces are 0 as well, so the load at k+1 is 0 either way — which is what the original produces. This holds at every assertion, not only at start-up (checked against the impulse_probe sequence, where rzerol correctly blocks the clear on the first post-impulse cycle and the block yields 127 = 255 mod 128, matching the reference). The added rzerol flops start X; if (reset) with X takes the load branch in int_sop_4.v:41, and the 8-cycle all-zero lead-in (tb_equiv_bilin.v:216-219) clears the blocks before cmp is set, so no initial value is relied upon.
  • Tie-offs and ports. All ports connected by name, mode_sigs=12'b0, chainin=64'b0, unused dx/dy tied to 0, chainout connected to a wire nothing reads.
  • Left regions. The nine matmult products (335-343) are 16×16 and their sums are of truncated slices am11[30:15]+am12[30:15]+am13[30:15] (348-350) — both reasons verified in the source.
  • Required statements. All regions accounted for (nine converted, nine left with a shared reason), blocks added (3) and tiles (6, the same figure the measured kept candidate reports), longest block series in a stage (one, 2.219 ns) against the slowest stage (4.635 ns soft path), the soft logic leaving each stage with the note that none is the slowest, and the before/after register stages (2 and 2) for the converted regions.

1	// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
4	// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
15	// X until the first clear.
16	module int_sop_4 (
17	    input clk,
18	    input reset,
19	    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
20	    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
21	    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
22	    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
23	    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
24	    input [63:0] chainin,
25	    output reg [63:0] result,
26	    output [63:0] chainout
27	);
28	
29	    // stage 1: the input registers
30	    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
31	    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;
32	
33	    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
34	    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
35	    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
36	    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
37	    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
38	    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64
39	
40	    always @(posedge clk) begin
41	        if (reset) begin
42	            result <= 0;
43	            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
44	            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
45	        end
46	        else begin
47	            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
48	            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
49	            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
50	        end
51	    end
52	
53	    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers
54	
55	endmodule

Task

Edit raygentop.v in this directory to carry out the approved plan below: rewrite the regions it names onto the hard block described next. If a step cannot be done as the plan says, stop and say which step and why; do not improvise a different rewrite.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.
The design
  • Regions in the approved plan: bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2874$348, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2875$349, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2876$350, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2877$351, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2878$352, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2879$353, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2880$354, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2881$355, bilinearintrp.$mul$raygentop.v:2882$356. The plan names their shared sum as 'bilinearintrp's three output sums — r = i1r+i2r+i3r (line 2884), g = i1g+i2g+i3g (2885), b = i1b+i2b+i3b (2886); three products per sum, one block per sum, no chaining'. In the design their products are registered 1 stage(s) before the sum.
Correctness: these must hold
  • Same behavior. The rewritten design must produce the same outputs as the original on every cycle, with every register of the original starting at 0. Do not change what the design computes. Logic added only to reproduce it (recomputing a value, deriving the block's reset, correcting a block's result) is allowed.
  • Visibility. Only what the block's output ports carry is visible outside it. A value read by anything else (another expression, a module port, another module) cannot go inside a block: keep it outside, or recompute it. Check the source for every reader.
  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.
  • Registers and reset. The block's registers, if it has any, behave as the contract states. A design register may become a block register only if that keeps its behavior. Drive the block's reset so that "same behavior" holds after every reset, not only at start-up. Registers the rewrite adds start unknown; do not rely on their initial value.
  • Assumptions. If the rewrite is correct only under an assumption about the design's inputs or use (a bound on a value, when a signal is asserted), state it on a line starting ASSUMES: and cite the lines of the design that support it. The reference testbench does not know your assumption, so the rewrite must still match the original under it.
  • Scope. Change only what the rewrite onto the block needs.
How to work

  • check.sh reads the architecture's declaration of every hard block. Instantiate the block by its name and do not declare it in the design: a design that defines a module of the block's name fails the check.

PLAN:

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 2). Same three blocks, same three sums, same two-cycle latency and the same reset derivation; what changes is the algebra used to fit the sums onto the block, so that every operand is 7 bits, the shared ~u bus and its inverter level disappear, and bit 7 of u/v becomes dead.

Why the new grouping. r is output[6:0] (line 2786) and is read only as blr/blg/blb, 7-bit wires (lines 1990-1992, 2011-2012), so only the low 7 bits of the sum are visible. A product's low 7 bits depend only on its operands' low 7 bits, so every operand may be reduced mod 128, and 255 ≡ 127 (mod 128). Hence

u*ru + v*rv + (255-u-v)rw ≡ u(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw (mod 128),

with all of u, v, ru-rw, rv-rw, rw taken as 7-bit values. The block's result is unsigned modulo 2^64, so result[6:0] equals the original r exactly; the difference lives entirely in bits 7 and above, which nothing reads. No ASSUMES is needed: this is an identity, not a bound on the inputs.

Against the kept version (ax=u, by=128+rv-rw, cx=~u) this removes: the 8-bit ~u bus that fed cx of all three blocks (24 DSP pin connections and ~8 inverter LUTs, and with them one LUT level on a path that ends at a block input register), one bit from every operand bus into the three tiles, and the three 8-bit 128+rv-rw adders (replaced by 7-bit subtracts). It costs three extra 7-bit subtracts (ru-rw per colour). All six subtracts sit on the weight inputs, which are slices of shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in (line 676), a top-level input pad, so they are on untimed pad-to-register paths and add nothing to any timed stage.

Edit (replacing lines 2794-2886 of bilinearintrp; everything else in the file is untouched). Keep reg[7:0] u; reg[7:0] v; and the combinational case (selectuv) block exactly as they are. Delete the declarations of ul, vl, wl, i1b..i3r, rul..bwl and the whole always @(posedge clk) product block and the three assign sums, and put in their place:

                        .result(gres), .chainout(gchain)) ;
        int_sop_4 bsop (.clk(clk), .reset(brst), .mode_sigs(12'b0),
                        .ax({2'b00, u[6:0]}), .ay({2'b00, buw}),
                        .bx({2'b00, v[6:0]}), .by({2'b00, bvw}),
                        .cx(9'b001111111), .cy({2'b00, bw}),
                        .dx(9'b0), .dy(9'b0), .chainin(64'b0),
                        .result(bres), .chainout(bchain)) ;

        assign r = rres[6:0] ;
        assign g = gres[6:0] ;
        assign b = bres[6:0] ;

Reset. reset is driven by rrst = rzero & rzerol, asserted when a colour's three weights were zero before each of the last two edges. The block then clears its operand and result registers; the value they would otherwise have loaded is the same: with ru=rv=rw=0 all three of ay=ruw, by=rvw, cy=rw are zero, so every product is zero and the result is zero either way, and the original's r for those cycles is zero too. This holds at every reset, not only at start-up, and it holds for the cycle after a reset as well (the cleared operand registers would have held zero weights). The testbench's 8-cycle all-zero lead-in (tb_equiv_bilin.v, LEAD_IN) asserts it before the first compared cycle, which is what flushes the blocks' unknown power-up state; the three added rzerol flip-flops are allowed to start unknown because the condition only ever fires when the weights have been zero on the current cycle too, and a spurious early clear writes the correct value 0.

Every candidate region.

  • The nine bilinearintrp products (lines 2874-2882) are all converted, three per block, one block per colour sum.
  • The nine matmult products (lines 335-343) are all left, for one shared reason: they are 16x16 and the block's ports are 9 bits, so each product would need four 8x8 partial products weighted by 1, 2^8 and 2^16, and the block cannot shift an operand or a partial product — the weighting would have to be done in soft adders outside, and each single multiply would need more than one tile. On top of that, matmult's sums are of truncated slices (am11[30:15] + am12[30:15] + am13[30:15], line 348), not of the products themselves, so the three products of a sum cannot be added inside one block even if they fitted: the low 15 bits each product contributes must be discarded before the add. Their products already sit on DSP tiles, so there is nothing to recover there either.

Blocks and tiles. 3 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three mult_9x9_fixed_pt tiles that held the same nine products: 6 DSP tiles in the design, unchanged from the baseline's 6.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. chainin is tied to 0 on all three blocks and no chainout is read, because the three colour sums are independent — chaining them would add the sums together. The stage the rewrite creates and its parts: u01a..v10c register clock-to-Q 0.060, wire into the 6:1 mux, two LUT levels for the mux (cell plus wire, about 1.0 each on this design), and 0.019 setup at the block input register, roughly 3.4 ns; inside the block 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns; out of the block 0.060 plus wire into linearmap and the colour readers, well under 1 ns of soft logic after it. Every one of these is below the design's slowest stage, which the rewrite does not touch — at seed 1 of the kept measurement that stage was a soft path of 4.635 ns (register, two adder chains, three LUT levels, register) with no block on it, and the matmult multiply stage is the other contender. The kept version's ~u inverter put a third LUT level on the mux-to-block stage; removing it shortens that stage by about one soft level (~0.9 ns including its wire), so if any seed's critical path ran through it, that seed's period falls; no stage gets longer.

Soft logic that leaves, and from which stage. Out of the stage that ran mux → operand latches: the ul, vl and wl registers and the 8-bit 255 - u - v subtract, and the nine 7-bit weight latches rul..bwl. Out of the stage that ran latch → multiply → product register: the nine product registers (7 bits each after the design's own trimming). Out of the stage that ran product register → sum → readers: the six 7-bit adders of the three sums. Added in their place: six 7-bit subtracts on the pad-driven weight inputs (untimed), three flip-flops and three 21-bit OR reductions for the reset. None of these stages is the design's slowest, so the gain here is area and wirelength, not period. Narrowing ax/bx to u[6:0]/v[6:0] also makes bit 7 of u and v dead: the mux bit for it goes away, and because u01a..v10c are read nowhere but this instance (declared at 1925-1937, passed only to line 2012), bit 7 of those twelve registers in resultrecieve is dead too and is removed by synthesis.

Register stages, before and after, for each converted region. Before: operands u/v/weights → stage 1 registers (ul, vl, wl, rul..bwl) → stage 2 registers (i1r..i3b, the products) → combinational 2-level adder → r/g/b. Two register stages, the sum combinational after them. After: operands → the block's input register (stage 1) → the block's result register (stage 2) → r/g/b combinational from result[6:0]. Two register stages, same latency, same cycle-by-cycle values.

Simulation

When you finish, the framework simulates your edited design against the original with the reference testbench, comparing every output on every cycle, on its own copy. The testbench (tb_equiv_bilin.v) and the block's behavioural model (int_sop_4.v) are in sim_reference/; you may read them, but editing them has no effect on the result.

In their place: the six 7-bit difference wires ruw/rvw/guw/gvw/buw/bvw, the zero-detect wires and their latches rzerol/gzerol/bzerol, the three reset wires, and the result/chainout wires.

The nine regions (was raygentop.v:2874-2882) and their three sums (2884-2886). Replaced by three int_sop_4 instances, one per colour sum, no chaining:

  • :2880$354, :2881$355, :2882$356 (the b products) → block bsop, b = bres[6:0].

Each block uses ax={2'b00,u[6:0]}, ay={2'b00,ruw}, bx={2'b00,v[6:0]}, by={2'b00,rvw}, cx=9'b001111111, cy={2'b00,rw}, dx=dy=9'b0, chainin=64'b0, mode_sigs=12'b0 (and the g/b equivalents). Every input port is connected; the unused product term d is tied to 0; chainout goes to a wire nothing reads.

Algebra. r/g/b are 7-bit outputs, so only the low 7 bits of each sum are visible; mod 128, u*ru + v*rv + (255-u-v)*rw == u*(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw. The six added 7-bit wrapping subtracts replace the 8-bit 255-u-v. The block's result is unsigned mod 2^64, so result[6:0] is exactly the original value; the difference is confined to bits 7 and up, which nothing reads. This is an identity, so no ASSUMES: line is needed.

Latency and reset. Operands → block input register → result register reproduces the original's two stages (ul/rul latches, then the product registers) with the sum folded in, so values match cycle for cycle. reset is driven by rrst = rzero & rzerol, high when a colour's three weights were zero before each of the last two edges; the cleared value equals what the block would otherwise have loaded (every y operand of that colour is 0, so every product and the result are 0 either way), at start-up and at every later reset alike. The three added rzerol flip-flops start unknown; the condition only fires when the weights are zero on the current cycle too, so an early spurious clear writes the correct 0.

The nine matmult products at raygentop.v:335-343 are left as soft $mul, as the plan specifies.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Inner-loop check: the front end of the real flow, then a cell census. NOT place-and-route.
# usage: bash check.sh <file.v>
# Reads, in the flow's order: blocks.vlib (every hard block of the architecture, declared from its
# models), primitives.vlib (the flow's library of memories, adders and multipliers), then the design;
# then elaborates with the flow's hierarchy check. A module that is not defined, a port name the
# block does not have, or a misspelled block name fails here as it would in the flow. Do not
# declare the target block in the design: blocks.vlib declares it, and a design that defines a module
# of the target block's name fails this check.
# Prints one pass/fail line, then the cell census of the whole design (the last "Number of cells"
# table yosys prints): soft arithmetic as $mul/$add/$sub, registers as $dff*/$sdff*, memories as
# $mem*, muxes as $mux/$pmux, and every instantiated module by name, which is where a hard-block
# instantiation shows up with its instance count.
set -u
f="${1:?usage: check.sh <file.v>}"
here="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
lib=""
[ -f "$here/blocks.vlib" ] && lib="read_verilog -lib $here/blocks.vlib; "
[ -f "$here/primitives.vlib" ] && lib="${lib}read_verilog -nomem2reg $here/primitives.vlib; "
target="$(sed -n 's|^// target block: *\([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_$]*\).*|\1|p' "$here/blocks.vlib" 2>/dev/null | head -1)"
if [ -n "$target" ] && grep -Eq "^[[:space:]]*module[[:space:]]+$target([^A-Za-z0-9_$]|$)" "$f"; then
  echo "FAIL: $f defines module $target; blocks.vlib declares it. Remove the module definition and keep the instances."
  exit 1
fi
out="$(yosys -p "${lib}read_verilog -sv -nolatches $f; hierarchy -check -auto-top -purge_lib; proc; opt; stat" 2>&1)"
rc=$?
if [ $rc -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "FAIL: does not synthesize (yosys exit $rc)"
  echo "$out" | grep -iE 'error|warning' | tail -15
  echo "$out" | tail -10
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: synthesizes cleanly"
echo "Cell census (yosys stat, whole design):"
echo "$out" | awk '/Number of cells:/{buf=$0 "\n"; on=1; next}
                   on && /^[[:space:]]+[$A-Za-z_][^[:space:]]*[[:space:]]+[0-9]+[[:space:]]*$/ {buf=buf $0 "\n"; next}
                   on {on=0}
                   END{printf "%s", buf}' \
  | grep -E 'Number of cells|^[[:space:]]+(\$(mul|add|sub|mem|memrd|memwr|dff|dffe|sdff|sdffe|adff|adffe|mux|pmux)|[A-Za-z_])' || true

// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
// inputs).
// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
// X until the first clear.
module int_sop_4 (
    input clk,
    input reset,
    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
    input [63:0] chainin,
    output reg [63:0] result,
    output [63:0] chainout
);

You are the acceptance reviewer. You did not plan or write this edit. Check the edit against the approved plan, the block's contract and the correctness rules.

The block
  • primitive to instantiate: int_sop_4 (precision INT9)
  • computes: out = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin
  • input ports: clk[1] (clock), reset[1], mode_sigs[12], ax[9], ay[9], bx[9], by[9], cx[9], cy[9], dx[9], dy[9], chainin[64]
  • output ports: result[64], chainout[64]
  • arithmetic: the block reads each operand port as an unsigned number, and its result is unsigned. An operand narrower than its port is zero-extended to the port width. The result wraps at 64 bits: a value past the result width keeps its low 64 bits (modulo 2^64), with no saturation and no flag.
  • registers: on clk, the block registers its operands (ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy) at one clock edge and result at the next, with the arithmetic between the two registers: operands applied before clock edge k appear in result after edge k+1, 2 cycles later. The block has no clock enable and no path around either register. chainin is registered at the block's entry like an operand and reaches result 2 cycles after it is applied. chainout is combinational from the input registers: it carries the value result loads at the next clock edge, one cycle before result shows it.
  • reset: reset is synchronous and active high: at a clock edge that samples it high it clears every register of the block (the operand registers, the chainin register and the result register) to 0, and the block loads again at the next edge that samples it low.
  • power-up: every register of the block is unknown until the first clear by reset; no register of the block has an initial value, and a rewrite may not rely on one.
  • tie-off: chainin = 0 when the block is not chained (a dedicated chain input: only another block's chainout or a constant may drive it); mode_sigs = 0 always (the architecture gives the port no meaning for this mode).
  • connections: connect every input port, by the port names above; a product-term port the rewrite does not use is tied to 0. chainout reaches only the next block's chainin, through a dedicated connection to the block directly below it in the column; it has no connection to general routing, so nothing else may read it.

  • Terms. Keep every term of the original arithmetic. A term with no matching block port is computed outside the block. A port the design ties to a constant may be tied the same way on the block.

PLAN:

This is a revision of the kept candidate (revision 2). Same three blocks, same three sums, same two-cycle latency and the same reset derivation; what changes is the algebra used to fit the sums onto the block, so that every operand is 7 bits, the shared ~u bus and its inverter level disappear, and bit 7 of u/v becomes dead.

Why the new grouping. r is output[6:0] (line 2786) and is read only as blr/blg/blb, 7-bit wires (lines 1990-1992, 2011-2012), so only the low 7 bits of the sum are visible. A product's low 7 bits depend only on its operands' low 7 bits, so every operand may be reduced mod 128, and 255 ≡ 127 (mod 128). Hence

u*ru + v*rv + (255-u-v)rw ≡ u(ru-rw) + v*(rv-rw) + 127*rw (mod 128),

with all of u, v, ru-rw, rv-rw, rw taken as 7-bit values. The block's result is unsigned modulo 2^64, so result[6:0] equals the original r exactly; the difference lives entirely in bits 7 and above, which nothing reads. No ASSUMES is needed: this is an identity, not a bound on the inputs.

Against the kept version (ax=u, by=128+rv-rw, cx=~u) this removes: the 8-bit ~u bus that fed cx of all three blocks (24 DSP pin connections and ~8 inverter LUTs, and with them one LUT level on a path that ends at a block input register), one bit from every operand bus into the three tiles, and the three 8-bit 128+rv-rw adders (replaced by 7-bit subtracts). It costs three extra 7-bit subtracts (ru-rw per colour). All six subtracts sit on the weight inputs, which are slices of shadedata = tm3_sram_data_in (line 676), a top-level input pad, so they are on untimed pad-to-register paths and add nothing to any timed stage.

Edit (replacing lines 2794-2886 of bilinearintrp; everything else in the file is untouched). Keep reg[7:0] u; reg[7:0] v; and the combinational case (selectuv) block exactly as they are. Delete the declarations of ul, vl, wl, i1b..i3r, rul..bwl and the whole always @(posedge clk) product block and the three assign sums, and put in their place:

Reset. reset is driven by rrst = rzero & rzerol, asserted when a colour's three weights were zero before each of the last two edges. The block then clears its operand and result registers; the value they would otherwise have loaded is the same: with ru=rv=rw=0 all three of ay=ruw, by=rvw, cy=rw are zero, so every product is zero and the result is zero either way, and the original's r for those cycles is zero too. This holds at every reset, not only at start-up, and it holds for the cycle after a reset as well (the cleared operand registers would have held zero weights). The testbench's 8-cycle all-zero lead-in (tb_equiv_bilin.v, LEAD_IN) asserts it before the first compared cycle, which is what flushes the blocks' unknown power-up state; the three added rzerol flip-flops are allowed to start unknown because the condition only ever fires when the weights have been zero on the current cycle too, and a spurious early clear writes the correct value 0.

Every candidate region.

  • The nine bilinearintrp products (lines 2874-2882) are all converted, three per block, one block per colour sum.
  • The nine matmult products (lines 335-343) are all left, for one shared reason: they are 16x16 and the block's ports are 9 bits, so each product would need four 8x8 partial products weighted by 1, 2^8 and 2^16, and the block cannot shift an operand or a partial product — the weighting would have to be done in soft adders outside, and each single multiply would need more than one tile. On top of that, matmult's sums are of truncated slices (am11[30:15] + am12[30:15] + am13[30:15], line 348), not of the products themselves, so the three products of a sum cannot be added inside one block even if they fitted: the low 15 bits each product contributes must be discarded before the add. Their products already sit on DSP tiles, so there is nothing to recover there either.

Blocks and tiles. 3 blocks, each taking a DSP tile alone, replacing the three mult_9x9_fixed_pt tiles that held the same nine products: 6 DSP tiles in the design, unchanged from the baseline's 6.

Longest series of blocks in a stage. One. chainin is tied to 0 on all three blocks and no chainout is read, because the three colour sums are independent — chaining them would add the sums together. The stage the rewrite creates and its parts: u01a..v10c register clock-to-Q 0.060, wire into the 6:1 mux, two LUT levels for the mux (cell plus wire, about 1.0 each on this design), and 0.019 setup at the block input register, roughly 3.4 ns; inside the block 0.060 + 2.140 + 0.019 = 2.219 ns; out of the block 0.060 plus wire into linearmap and the colour readers, well under 1 ns of soft logic after it. Every one of these is below the design's slowest stage, which the rewrite does not touch — at seed 1 of the kept measurement that stage was a soft path of 4.635 ns (register, two adder chains, three LUT levels, register) with no block on it, and the matmult multiply stage is the other contender. The kept version's ~u inverter put a third LUT level on the mux-to-block stage; removing it shortens that stage by about one soft level (~0.9 ns including its wire), so if any seed's critical path ran through it, that seed's period falls; no stage gets longer.

Soft logic that leaves, and from which stage. Out of the stage that ran mux → operand latches: the ul, vl and wl registers and the 8-bit 255 - u - v subtract, and the nine 7-bit weight latches rul..bwl. Out of the stage that ran latch → multiply → product register: the nine product registers (7 bits each after the design's own trimming). Out of the stage that ran product register → sum → readers: the six 7-bit adders of the three sums. Added in their place: six 7-bit subtracts on the pad-driven weight inputs (untimed), three flip-flops and three 21-bit OR reductions for the reset. None of these stages is the design's slowest, so the gain here is area and wirelength, not period. Narrowing ax/bx to u[6:0]/v[6:0] also makes bit 7 of u and v dead: the mux bit for it goes away, and because u01a..v10c are read nowhere but this instance (declared at 1925-1937, passed only to line 2012), bit 7 of those twelve registers in resultrecieve is dead too and is removed by synthesis.

Register stages, before and after, for each converted region. Before: operands u/v/weights → stage 1 registers (ul, vl, wl, rul..bwl) → stage 2 registers (i1r..i3b, the products) → combinational 2-level adder → r/g/b. Two register stages, the sum combinational after them. After: operands → the block's input register (stage 1) → the block's result register (stage 2) → r/g/b combinational from result[6:0]. Two register stages, same latency, same cycle-by-cycle values.

DESIGN_CHANGE: matmult would map onto this block if its operands were 9 bits or narrower, or if Cx/Cy/Cz were formed by truncating the sum of the three full products rather than by summing three truncated slices of them (line 348) — the latter alone would let a 9-bit-operand version put each of its three-product sums on a single block.

ACCEPT

Checked against the plan and the rules:

  • Plan fidelity — the edit replaces exactly lines 2794–2886 of bilinearintrp as the plan specifies: reg[7:0] u/v and the case (selectuv) mux kept verbatim (raygentop.v:2794-2858), the old ul/vl/wl, rul..bwl, i1r..i3b declarations and the product always block and three sums removed, and the six subtracts, three zero-detects, three rzerol flops, three resets and three int_sop_4 instances put in their place (raygentop.v:2860-2907). Nothing outside the module changed — matmult's products at raygentop.v:335-343 are intact, exactly 3 int_sop_4 instances exist, and the harness subtree check (sim_run.log:3) confirms the rest of the file is unchanged.
  • Ports — every input of each instance is connected by name: clk, reset, mode_sigs(12'b0), ax/ay/bx/by/cx/cy, unused dx/dy tied to 9'b0, chainin(64'b0). result[6:0] drives r/g/b; chainout goes to rchain/gchain/bchain, which nothing reads, as the plan states.
  • Terms and visibility — all three products of each colour sum are inside the block. r/g/b are output[6:0] (2786-2791) and their only readers are the 7-bit blr/blg/blb (1990-1992, 2011-2012, 2265-2267, 2423-2425, 2482-2484), so only bits 6:0 are visible. Mod 128, ul*rul + vl*rvl + wl*rwl with wl = 255-u-v equals u[6:0]*(ru-rw) + v[6:0]*(rv-rw) + 127*rw; all three subtracts are 7-bit wrapping in self-determined context, so the identity is exact, not a bound on the inputs — no ASSUMES is owed. The removed ul/wl/rul..bwl are module-local; the ul at 2706 belongs to a different module.
  • Registers and reset — operands are registered at one edge and result at the next, matching the original's ul/rul → i1r two-stage pipeline (nonblocking, so i1r uses the previous ul). rrst = rzero & rzerol only fires when the weights were zero on both the current and previous cycle, so the cleared operand registers would have held zero weights and the cleared result would have loaded 0 anyway: the clear is a no-op at every reset, not just at start-up. The added rzerol flops may power up X — reset then reads X, int_sop_4.v:41 takes the else branch, and the clear simply lands one edge later; no reliance on an initial value, and the sim reports x_on_dut_only = 0.

1	// int_sop_4: result = ax*ay + bx*by + cx*cy + dx*dy + chainin, unsigned, each 9x9 product
2	// zero-extended into a 64-bit sum, modulo 2^64 (the sum wraps at the result width).
3	// Ports: clk, reset, mode_sigs[12], ax, ay, bx, by, cx, cy, dx, dy [9 each], chainin[64] in;
4	// result[64], chainout[64] out. mode_sigs is not read.
5	// Registers (the arch's annotation read literally, decision 2026-10-16): every input is registered
6	// at the block's entry at one clock edge (the eight operands and chainin alike); the
7	// products and their sum are formed from those registers and loaded into result at the next edge.
8	// Cycles: every operand and chainin to result 2. chainout is combinational from the input
9	// registers: the sum result loads at the next edge unless that edge clears it (1 cycle from the
10	// inputs).
11	// Reset: synchronous, active high (2026-10-17: the arch's annotation does not distinguish a reset
12	// register from a clear sampled by the registers themselves): at a clock edge that samples it high
13	// every register of the block (operand registers, chainin register, result) is cleared to 0; the block
14	// loads again at the next edge that samples it low. No register has an initial value: every one is
15	// X until the first clear.
16	module int_sop_4 (
17	    input clk,
18	    input reset,
19	    input [11:0] mode_sigs,
20	    input [8:0] ax, input [8:0] ay,
21	    input [8:0] bx, input [8:0] by,
22	    input [8:0] cx, input [8:0] cy,
23	    input [8:0] dx, input [8:0] dy,
24	    input [63:0] chainin,
25	    output reg [63:0] result,
26	    output [63:0] chainout
27	);
28	
29	    // stage 1: the input registers
30	    reg [8:0]  ax_reg, ay_reg, bx_reg, by_reg, cx_reg, cy_reg, dx_reg, dy_reg;
31	    reg [63:0] chainin_reg;
32	
33	    // combinational middle: the four products and their sum, from the registers
34	    wire [17:0] prod_a = ax_reg * ay_reg;                        // 9x9 -> 18, exact
35	    wire [17:0] prod_b = bx_reg * by_reg;
36	    wire [17:0] prod_c = cx_reg * cy_reg;
37	    wire [17:0] prod_d = dx_reg * dy_reg;
38	    wire [63:0] sum    = prod_a + prod_b + prod_c + prod_d + chainin_reg;   // modulo 2^64
39	
40	    always @(posedge clk) begin
41	        if (reset) begin
42	            result <= 0;
43	            ax_reg <= 0; ay_reg <= 0; bx_reg <= 0; by_reg <= 0;
44	            cx_reg <= 0; cy_reg <= 0; dx_reg <= 0; dy_reg <= 0; chainin_reg <= 0;
45	        end
46	        else begin
47	            ax_reg <= ax; ay_reg <= ay; bx_reg <= bx; by_reg <= by;
48	            cx_reg <= cx; cy_reg <= cy; dx_reg <= dx; dy_reg <= dy; chainin_reg <= chainin;
49	            result <= sum;                                       // stage 2
50	        end
51	    end
52	
53	    assign chainout = sum;                                  // the sum of the input registers
54	
55	endmodule

+ // u*ru + v*rv + wl*rw, with wl = 255-u-v, regrouped onto one sum-of-products block
+ // per colour: u*ru + v*(128+rv-rw) + (255-u)*rw, which differs from the original
+ // sum by 128*v only and so agrees on the low 7 bits the module outputs.
+ assign rvc = (8'b10000000 + {1'b0, rv}) - {1'b0, rw} ;
+ assign gvc = (8'b10000000 + {1'b0, gv}) - {1'b0, gw} ;
+ assign bvc = (8'b10000000 + {1'b0, bv}) - {1'b0, bw} ;
+
+ // the blocks power up unknown, so clear them whenever a colour's weights have been
+ // zero for two cycles: the value the block would load is then 0 anyway

+ assign gzero = ~(|{gu, gv, gw}) ;
+ assign bzero = ~(|{bu, bv, bw}) ;

layout koios_extra_small · used area 4.7578e+06 · critical path 4.84712 ns · wirelength 25664 · area x delay x wirelength (delay register to register, 2026-10-20) 5.91854e+11 (read from entry; median per term over the entry's seed runs (its seed_medians; seeds lists them))

The objective is area x delay x wirelength (delay register to register, 2026-10-20): VPR's total used logic block area (I/Os and empty grid tiles excluded) times the critical path times the total routed wirelength. Each term is the median over the loop's seeds; the product is the product of the medians. Beside every product stand the ratios against the baseline, A/A0 (area), D/D0 (critical path), W/W0 (wirelength) and their product, so the normalization can be read off. After each measured rewrite, the planner is given every measurement so far and asked for a revision. A revision is built and checked like the first rewrite, and the lowest product is kept, a later rewrite having to beat it by more than 4.32%. The loop stops when the planner declines to revise, when a revision does not lower the best product by more than 4.32%, when a revision fails its checks, or when 9 revisions have been made.

Stated: the BLOCKS, TILES and STAGE_NS lines of the plan header. Measured: the packed DSP tile count from the gate flow, and the median period, area and wirelength over the seeds. "A/A0 · D/D0 · W/W0" are the rewrite's medians over the baseline's, whose product is the "vs baseline" change plus one. "vs previous" is against the rewrite measured before this one. "Path 1 ends in" is read from the rewrite's own timing report and netlist: the constant coefficients on the block (or plain multiply) that path 1 passes through, matched against the constants each module of the edited RTL multiplies by; two modules that share a coefficient set are both named, and the hover text gives the element and its constants. Verification comes from verification.yaml in the run dir when one was written; the loop itself does not run the equivalence checks. Its label is proven when the LEC closed, simulation under assumption when the simulation passed without a closed proof and the plan stated a bound it rests on, simulation only when it stated none; the hover text gives the simulation and LEC results and the stated bounds.

+ // u*ru + v*rv + wl*rw, with wl = 255-u-v, regrouped onto one sum-of-products block
+ // per colour: u*ru + v*(128+rv-rw) + (255-u)*rw, which differs from the original
+ // sum by 128*v only and so agrees on the low 7 bits the module outputs.
+ assign rvc = (8'b10000000 + {1'b0, rv}) - {1'b0, rw} ;
+ assign gvc = (8'b10000000 + {1'b0, gv}) - {1'b0, gw} ;
+ assign bvc = (8'b10000000 + {1'b0, bv}) - {1'b0, bw} ;
+
+ // the blocks power up unknown, so clear them whenever a colour's weights have been
+ // zero for two cycles: the value the block would load is then 0 anyway
+ assign rzero = ~(|{ru, rv, rw}) ;
+ assign gzero = ~(|{gu, gv, gw}) ;
+ assign bzero = ~(|{bu, bv, bw}) ;
+
always @(posedge clk)
begin
- wl <= 8'b11111111 - u - v ;
- ul <= u ;
- vl <= v ;
- rul <= ru ;
- rvl <= rv ;
- rwl <= rw ;

- gvl <= gv ;
- gwl <= gw ;
- bul <= bu ;
- bvl <= bv ;
- bwl <= bw ;
- i1r <= ul * rul ;
- i2r <= vl * rvl ;
- i3r <= wl * rwl ;
- i1g <= ul * gul ;
- i2g <= vl * gvl ;
- i3g <= wl * gwl ;
- i1b <= ul * bul ;
- i2b <= vl * bvl ;
- i3b <= wl * bwl ;
1 whitespace-only line (indentation or trailing spaces changed, text identical)
- end
- assign r = (i1r + i2r + i3r) ;
- assign g = (i1g + i2g + i3g) ;
- assign b = (i1b + i2b + i3b) ;
+ rzerol <= rzero ;
+ gzerol <= gzero ;
+ bzerol <= bzero ;
1 whitespace-only line (indentation or trailing spaces changed, text identical)
+ end
+
+ assign rrst = rzero & rzerol ;
